Advanced Data Reduction

Dell.com Contact Us
Share
United States/English

Home > Storage > PowerMax and VMAX > White Papers > A Detailed Overview of the Next Generation PowerMax Platform > Advanced Data Reduction

Advanced Data Reduction

  • PowerMaxOS delivers data reduction using proven Adaptive Compression Engine (ACE) and inline deduplication to provide and industry leading 5:1 data reduction guarantee for Open Systems block data and the industry’s only 3:1 data reduction guarantee for Mainframe data.

    Data Reduction allows users to present more front-end effective capacity while utilizing  lower backend usable capacity. PowerMax data reduction includes both compression and dedupe operations. Compression reduces the size of data sets and dedupe identifies identical data sets and stores a single instance. The system uses both functions together to achieve its data deduction ratios.

    Data reduction on the PowerMax is an inline operation, performed by each nodes embedded DPU. Offloading these data reduction functions to the DPU allows the system to be capacity efficient and deliver exceptional capacity savings, while not incurring any noticeable performance impact to customer I/O operations.

    PowerMax data reduction is enabled at the storage group level. The feature is enabled by default when creating individual storage groups using either Unisphere for PowerMax, RESTAPI, or Solutions Enabler. The option to enable or disable data reduction for individual storage groups can be changed at any time using these tools.

    Data reduction using the Adaptive Compression Engine

    PowerMax employs inline hardware compression using the Adaptive Compression Engine (ACE). ACE provides PowerMax and VMAX All Flash customers with a data reduction method that provides negligible performance impact while delivering the highest space saving capability. The following design factors make the Dell EMC Adaptive Compression Engine unique:

    • Intelligent compression algorithms – Intelligent compression algorithms determine the best compression ratios to be used and provide the ability to dynamically modify storage backend layout for the highest data compression efficiencies.
    • Inline hardware data compression – Inline hardware data compression greatly inhibits the compression function from consuming critical PowerMax system core resources.
    • Activity Based Compression – Activity Based Compression (ABC) focuses the compression function on the least busy data in the system, while allowing the most active data in the system to bypass the compression workflow. This ensures that all data in the system receives the appropriate compression focus while maintaining optimal response time.
    • Fine Grain Data Packing – Fine Grain Data Packing which includes a zero reclaim function that prevents the allocation of buffers with all zeros or no actual data.
    • Enhanced Compression – There is an additional compression algorithm found in PowerMaxOS called Enhanced Compression (EC). The EC algorithm scans already compressed data which the system determines to have been not accessed for a long period of time. The EC algorithm then tries to further reduce this data, to a larger compression ratio, to realize additional capacity savings.

    Data reduction using inline deduplication.

    PowerMax employs inline hardware deduplication to identify repeated data patterns on the array and store those repeated patterns using a single instance in the array’s usable capacity. Depending on customer workloads, inline deduplication along with inline compression give PowerMax the ability to achieve an industry leading data reduction ratio with negligible performance impact. The following are the important design factors for deduplication on PowerMax:

    • Inline hardware data deduplication – Inline hardware-based data deduplication prevents the consumption of critical PowerMax system core resources, limiting performance impact. The deduplication and compression functions are performed on the same hardware module in the PowerMax system.
    • Deduplication Algorithm – PowerMax uses the SHA-2 algorithm to perform the deduplication function. The SHA-2 algorithm produces a unique data identifier for each item of data which is processed through the compression engine. These unique identifiers are stored in a Hash ID table on the PowerMax system.
    • Hash ID Table – The Hash ID table stores all the Hash IDs for the data processed through the compression engine. When a new write enters the compression engine, the Hash ID created for the write is compared to the Hash IDs already in the table. If the Hash ID is found to already exist in the Hash ID table, the write is not written to the storage.
    • Dedupe Management Object (DMO) – The DMO is a 64-byte object which serves as the connection (pointer) between the devices and the single instance of actual data. DMOs are stored in the PowerMax global cache.

    For more information about PowerMax Data Reduction consult the following white paper: Dell PowerMax Data Reduction

An End-to-End Cybersecurity Solution

  • The PowerMax cybersecurity model has been implemented from the storage to the application, and to the user of the system, providing customers with a complete end-to-end cybersecurity solution. The following figure illustrates the various components which comprise this end-to-end solution

    Primary components of the PowerMax cybersecurity end-to-end solution

    The PowerMax cybersecurity model provides a comprehensive solution that covers all aspects of security, from storage to application and user levels. This end-to-end approach ensures that customers receive a robust and integrated cybersecurity solution that safeguards their entire system.

Choice and Flexibility in Cloud Backups

  • One of the standout attributes of Storage Direct Protection is the choice and flexibility it provides customers regarding their cloud backup strategies. PowerProtect DDVE integrates with multiple cloud providers, including AWS, Azure, Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and Alibaba. This flexibility enables organizations to avoid vendor lock-in, allowing them to select the provider that best fits their business needs. Additionally, customers can mix on-premises and cloud data protection copies to build a robust multicloud data protection strategy, effectively adapting to changing requirements without being confined to a single vendor’s ecosystem.

    PowerMax Multicloud Data Protection Strategy

Cost-Effective Data Protection

  • Storage Direct Protection leverages the industry-leading capabilities of PowerProtect, widely recognized as the leading data protection appliance in the industry. Leveraging PowerProtect for this solution results in the following cost-related advantages:

    • Compatibility: The integration accommodates both physical PowerProtect Data Domain appliances and software-defined Data Domain Virtual Edition (DDVE).
    • Cost Reduction Strategies: By utilizing object storage, efficient data reduction, and bandwidth-efficient replication, organizations can significantly lower their data storage costs.

    The integration works seamlessly with both physical PowerProtect Data Domain appliances and software-defined Data Domain Virtual Edition (DDVE). The cost reduction strategies employed by this feature encompass various methods, including the use of object storage, efficient data reduction, and bandwidth-efficient replication, which collectively lower overall storage costs.

Detection and response

  • Being able to detect and quickly respond to threats is key to a successful security strategy. Apex AI Operations Observability (AAIOO) is a powerful application used to track system health through pattern recognition using Artificial Intelligence (AI) modelling. Through using PowerMax’s AIOps and AAIOO Cybersecurity together, users can define legal configurations for PowerMax, monitor the system, and receive alerts if the array is out of compliance. AAIOO works in conjunction with PowerMax AIOps to be able to track data patterns and detect anomalies, including changes to data reduction rates, to establish if ransomware or malware may have infected the system. Once suspicious anomalies are detected, AAIOO alerts IT management to take corrective action. PowerMax AIOps provides real-time visibility into network and system activity, allowing IT teams to detect potential security threats as they occur minimizing the risk of data loss or other security breaches.

Efficient Workload Consolidation

  • PowerMaxOS allows the next generation PowerMax platform to consolidate demanding mixed workloads all the while delivering consistently high levels of performance. PowerMax is the only platform in the industry in which a customer can run mainframe, open systems block, and file workloads natively on the same system without the use of additional hardware, gateways, or third-party solutions. This capability provides PowerMax’s customers with the following advantages:

    • Cost Efficiency: By allowing customers to run mainframe, open systems block, and file workloads natively on the same system without the need for additional hardware, gateways, or third-party solutions, PowerMax offers a cost-effective solution. This eliminates the expenses associated with purchasing and maintaining separate systems for different types of workloads. This reduces complexity in managing different systems and streamlines operations for the customer.
    • Scalability and Flexibility: PowerMax offers the flexibility to run diverse workloads on the same system, providing scalability for future growth and adaptability to changing business requirements without the need for significant additional investments in hardware or software.
    • Reliability and Security: With all workloads running on a single platform, PowerMax can potentially enhance reliability and security by centralizing management and monitoring processes. This can lead to better data protection and easier implementation of consistent security measures across all workloads.

    The following section details some of the specific mainframe and SDNAS capabilities that can only be found on the next generation PowerMax platform.

    Mainframe Enhancements

    Dell's ongoing commitment to supporting mainframe environments is exemplified by the latest enhancements found in every release of PowerMaxOS. Each update introduces several substantial improvements specifically designed for companies operating within mainframe workloads, reinforcing PowerMax's reputation as a reliable and cutting-edge solution for this unique market.

    Among the key advancements in the latest release of PowerMaxOS 10.2 is the significant increase in Input/Output Operations Per Second (IOPS) and the reduction of latency for mainframe workloads. This enhancement is achieved through improved support for unbalanced workloads, allowing additional processor capacity to be dynamically deployed where it is needed most. This capability is vital for organizations with fluctuating workload demands, ensuring that mainframe applications maintain optimal performance at all times. The introduction of zHyperlink performance reporting via Unisphere 10.2.0 further allows administrators to monitor zHyperlink resource consumption closely, which provides essential insights into workload performance and enables proactive management of mainframe operations.

    Dell enables mainframe workloads to be run on the entry-class PowerMax 2500 system, making advanced storage capabilities more accessible to a broader range of organizations. The PowerMax 2500 alongside the PowerMax 8500, are the first storage platforms in the industry to offer full mainframe data reduction, guaranteeing a 3:1 data reduction ratio for mainframe workloads. This feature not only optimizes storage efficiency but also improves overall cost-effectiveness for businesses managing substantial mainframe data.

    Another significant mainframe capability found on PowerMax is full end-to-end 32 Gb FICON support, which utilizes the same I/O modules as 32 Gb Fibre Channel for both the PowerMax 2500 and 8500. This eliminates the need for specialized FICON I/O modules, simplifying ordering, setup and maintenance while ensuring compatibility. Additionally, PowerMax now offers full hardware support for 64 Gb zHyperlink, further expanding the capabilities of mainframe workload management.

    Further emphasizing Dell's commitment to mainframe environments is the introduction of zCID, or cyber intrusion detection for mainframe workloads. This industry-first feature employs "auto-learning" access pattern detection for Storage Management Subsystem (SMS) storage groups, constructing detailed workload profiles that facilitate the creation of customized intrusion warning rules. With the ability to dynamically modify these rules based on evolving workload profiles, businesses gain enhanced visibility into potentially threatened storage groups, thereby empowering proactive intervention against security threats.

    Lastly, the latest release of PowerMaxOS10.2 leverages IBM’s System Recovery Boost technology, optimizing recovery operations within the mainframe server. This innovation significantly reduces processing time during configuration and critical recovery operations of Dell's Autoswap and Consistency Group for z/OS, which are essential for ensuring rapid recovery during both planned and unplanned outages. By minimizing downtime, Dell solidifies PowerMax’s role as a critical component in maintaining the resilience and reliability of mainframe workloads.

    The next generation PowerMax and the latest enhancements introduced in PowerMaxOS10.2 serve as a testament to Dell PowerMax's continuing support for mainframe environments. By improving mainframe performance metrics, enhancing security measures, and optimizing recovery capabilities, Dell reinforces its dedication to meeting the evolving needs of organizations that rely on mainframe systems. These advancements not only highlight PowerMax's robust capabilities but also empower businesses to operate more efficiently and securely in today’s complex data landscape, allowing them to confidently focus on their core business objectives while effectively managing their mainframe workloads.

    PowerMax File Enhancements

    The next generation PowerMax’s support Dell's Software-Defined Network Attached Storage (SDNAS) represents a significant leap forward in addressing the storage and management needs of modern organizations. The SDNAS architecture features an efficient 64-bit containerized microservice design that allows for lightweight deployment, ease of management, and rapid scaling of services. This modular approach improves performance and facilitates fast updates tailored to specific workloads.

    A key feature of the SDNAS architecture is the Single Global Namespace, which enables scalable file access across all nodes. This unifying approach simplifies data management by providing users with a single view of files, regardless of their storage location. This file platform can provide 4 data movers (containers acting as file servers) on the PowerMax 2500 and 8 data movers on the PowerMax 8500. Each data mover can provide users with up to 512 TB of usable capacity which can be carved up into the 64 TB (maximum) SMB or NFS file systems. Additionally, the active/active high availability architecture is scalable across two to sixteen nodes, ensuring continuous access to data even in the event of a node failure, thus providing reliability for mission-critical operations.

    Moreover, SDNAS includes full data service integration for services like SRDF/S and SRDF/A, TimeFinder SnapVX, Service Levels, Data Reduction, and Data at Rest Encryption (D@RE). These features enhance data integrity, optimize storage efficiency, and protect sensitive information while also supporting non-disruptive upgrades that allow organizations to improve their systems without experiencing downtime.

    Further enhancements allow SDNAS to share the same I/O module used for iSCSI, GbE SRDF, and NVMe/TCP connectivity, simplifying infrastructure requirements and reducing costs. This flexibility enables organizations to consolidate resources without compromising performance. Additionally, the native support for modern networking implementations, including VLANs and IPv6, ensures seamless integration with contemporary networking protocols, allowing for greater adaptability to evolving IT infrastructures.

    The following is a summary of the core SDNAS capabilities found on the next generation PowerMax Platform:

    • Efficient 64-bit containerized microservice architecture
    • Support up to 4 file servers on PowerMax 2500 and up to 8 file servers on PowerMax 8500
    • Active/active high availability architecture scalable across 2 -16 nodes
    • Single Global Namespace file access scalable across all nodes
    • 64 TB SMB and NFS file system support for traditional and transactional file workloads
    • Full data service integration for SRDF/S and SRDF/A, TimeFinder Snap, Service Levels, Data Reduction, D@RE, and Non disruptive upgrades
    • SDNAS can share the same I/O module that is used for iSCSI, GbE SRDF, and NVMe/TCP connectivity.
    • Native Support for modern networking implementations using VLANs and IPv6

    The advancements in Dell's SDNAS not only highlight the architecture's capacity for efficient storage and management but also reflect Dell's commitment to providing modern solutions that meet the diverse needs of organizations. As businesses increasingly seek to optimize their data management strategies, SDNAS emerges as a powerful tool that enhances efficiency, flexibility, and data accessibility in today's data-driven landscape.

Enhanced Automation/Infrastructure as Code (IaC)

  • To properly manage the modern data center, IT organizations need to focus on problem solving and not worry about routine and repeatable tasks that can be automated; furthermore, IT Operations Automation cannot be limited to simple scripting tasks just to save a few clicks. Automation needs to be well thought through and designed in a way that can scale across organizations, processes, and a hybrid cloud infrastructure. Dell offers a range of solutions to integrate with automation tools using the PowerMax REST API. These primary integrations are:

    • Ansible Collections for PowerMax: Ansible is a very popular configuration management platform to automate IT Operations and modern DevOps workflows. Dell Provide Ansible Collections for PowerMax available for download through Ansible Galaxy. These collections cover all major storage provisioning and data services configuration management via idempotent tasks that can be used to build comprehensive playbooks and roles. Sample Playbooks are available on the Dell GitHub here.
    • CSI-Driver and CSM Modules for Kubernetes (K8s), The CSI Drivers by Dell implement an interface between CSI enabled Container Orchestrator (CO) and Dell PowerMax and other Dell Storage Arrays. It is a plug-in that is installed into Kubernetes to provide persistent storage using the Dell storage system to containers. The Dell Technologies (Dell) Container Storage Modules (CSM) enables simple and consistent integration and automation experiences, extending enterprise storage capabilities to Kubernetes for cloud-native stateful applications. It reduces management complexity so developers can independently consume enterprise storage with ease and automate daily operations such as provisioning, snapshotting, replication, observability, authorization, application mobility, encryption, and resiliency. For more details, please refer to the official documentation here.

    PowerMax has well defined integration solutions that automate storage administration, provisioning, and consumption for the PowerMax storage platform. These modules enable the operations teams to rapidly provision storage infrastructure with accuracy to respond to the fast-paced needs of application developers.

    Note: For more information on using Dell EMC storage functionality through third-party tools and RESTAPIs, visit https://developer.dell.com/.

Enhanced monitoring and issue identification

  • PowerMaxOS AIOps integrates advanced capabilities designed for process monitoring and issue identification, enhancing the overall operational efficiency and reliability of the PowerMax storage platform. These robust AIOps features utilize artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies to analyze system performance, predict potential issues, and automate responses, thereby minimizing downtime and operational disruption.

    One of the primary advantages of AIOps within PowerMaxOS is its proficiency in real-time monitoring of system processes. By continuously assessing various metrics, such as IOPS, latency, and resource utilization, AIOps can swiftly detect anomalies that may signify underlying issues. This proactive monitoring ensures that organizations can address problems before they escalate, thereby maintaining high performance and service levels.

    Additionally, the issue identification capabilities of AIOps allow for comprehensive diagnostics. When an anomaly is detected, the system can analyze historical data and current performance trends to help pinpoint the root cause of the issue. This capability not only reduces the time spent on troubleshooting but also enhances the accuracy of problem resolution, allowing personnel to focus on strategic initiatives rather than become bogged down by routine monitoring tasks and problem-solving.

    PowerMax’s AIOps capabilities provide organizations with a powerful tool for robust process monitoring and issue identification. The following sections will provide some examples of this capability.

    Monitoring: storage process control using intelligent alerting thresholds.

    When a PowerMax system is brought online, the system starts collecting over 80 different performance metrics for minimum, maximum, and average values. Once the system has enough data to trend (15 days minimum), the system has the ability to suggest “intelligent thresholds” for key metrics based on machine learning applied to the measured trends. Using the PowerMax generated intelligent thresholds greatly enhances the effectiveness and responsiveness of the system by allowing for the creation of more accurate, actionable alerts that can notify when a process on the system is falling outside of threshold values which are defined from machine learning algorithms rather than those defined by user analysis.

    The following figure shows an example of using intelligent thresholds capabilities in Unisphere for PowerMax with upper and lower thresholds being displayed for a chart displaying system power consumption. When the measured metric value is within the upper and lower control limits, the system is operating as normal or in control. Alerts can be set to notify when the measured metric, in this example the power consumption of the system, deviate the control limits. When an alert is received in the case of storage power consumption exceeding the upper threshold value, the customer could start investigations and/or take corrective action such as offloading workloads from the system. Below is a Unisphere for PowerMax process control chart showing system power consumption along with intelligent upper and lower thresholds.

    Unisphere process control chart for power consumption using Intelligent thresholds

    The above chart showing the power consumption with the thresholds, along with other charts showing critical metrics, can be placed into a Unisphere dashboard, giving the user a single pane of glass monitoring view as to the overall health of the system

    Issue Identification

    PowerMax AIOps excels at not only monitoring the system, but also at clearly identifying issues and their root causes. This ability offers several key values to customers, including proactive issue identification, root cause analysis, efficiency, improved uptime, and increased visibility. By exceling at identifying issues and their root causes, PowerMax AIOps enables customers to take proactive measures to prevent downtime and minimize the impact on their business. Additionally, the solution's ability to quickly identify and resolve issues reduces the time and effort required to troubleshoot problems, freeing up IT teams to focus on more strategic activities. Furthermore, PowerMax AIOps provides customers with clear and actionable insights into their IT systems, enabling them to make data-driven decisions and optimize their infrastructure for better performance and reliability. An example of this capability is PowerMax’s support for Fabric Performance Impact Notifications (FPIN).

    PowerMax FPIN Integration

    FPINs are a critical enhancement for Fibre Channel SAN which greatly aids in the troubleshooting of fabric congestion issues. Being able to quickly identify, isolate, and resolve congestion or other issue impacting data flow is vital to maintaining the performance and reliability of the SAN. In standard FC, there was little in the way of proactively identifying problem data flows and then notifying the sending or receiving devices of the issue until a fabric wide event was unfolding. Prior to FPINs, FC SAN administrators would have to resort to various time consuming "heavy-handed" strategies such as resetting ports, manually forcing the discarding of frames on ports, and modifying fabric designs by allocating additional bandwidth to compensate congested flows effectively. Unfortunately, in many instances, these time-consuming approaches only addressed the symptoms without truly identifying and resolving the underlying issue.

    FPINs are part of a broader industry standard put forth by the Fibre Channel governing T11 committee called “Fabric Notifications”. FPINs are a mechanism that provides end devices with more information about events in the fabric – particularly around fabric congestion. Fabric Notifications were developed to optimize I/O behavior and avoid impaired paths by notifying devices on the SAN fabric of current overall fabric conditions. These notifications include detailed information about link integrity issues, delivery notification issues, congestion issues, and information about the source of the issue detailing which end point device on the fabric is the root cause the congestion. FPINs are sent out from the FC switch to all the end devices in the offending device’s peer zone group. To receive the FPIN, the endpoint hosts and storage systems must be enabled for FPIN awareness. FPINs make an end point device aware of the problem and the details. Depending on how FPINs have been implemented on the endpoint device, an alert is generated with the detailed information and is made visible to the administrators through various network management tools.

    As of the time of this writing, the next generation PowerMax is the industry’s only enterprise class storage array which supports FPIN integration into its storage architecture allowing it to provide critical alerts with detailed information as to the type and source of the fabric congestion to storage administrators. These FPINs alerts from the PowerMax system are displayed to the user through Unisphere for PowerMax, RESTAPI, Solutions Enabler, and through the Apex AIOPs Observability platform. Below is an example of a peer congestion FPIN alert being displayed in Solutions Enabler:

    FPIN alert display in Solutions Enabler

    The above output can help direct a user to quickly determining what type of congestion event is occurring and the location of the devices that are experiencing the congestion. This information in the FPIN alert can save SAN administrators hours of tedious fabric troubleshooting trying to identify where the problem exists on the fabric. The following figure shows how a similar FPIN alert appears in Unisphere. The same information as above can be gathered from the Unisphere output.

    FPIN alert display in Unisphere for PowerMax

    As shown with the above two examples, it clear that the AIOps capabilities of PowerMax provide organizations with a powerful tool for robust process monitoring and issue identification. By leveraging artificial intelligence and machine learning, PowerMax enables proactive management of storage environments, reduces downtime, and allows IT teams to concentrate on high-value tasks, ultimately contributing to a more efficient and reliable data management strategy.

    Note: For more information about FPINs and how they are implemented on PowerMax consult the following white paper: https://infohub.delltechnologies.com/nl-nl/t/fabric-notifications-with-dell-powermax/

Flexible RAID

  • The disaggregation of storage and compute in the next generation PowerMax architecture allows the PowerMax 2500 and 8500 to implement a new RAID distribution scheme called “Flexible RAID Technology” or “FlexRAID”. FlexRAID provides all compute nodes in the system with active-active access to the storage resources which are distributed across all the DMEs in the system. This model provides customers a far more efficient storage capacity solution by reducing the RAID overhead of the system allowing for higher system capacity using fewer drives, all the while delivering the highest levels of resiliency and data protection.

    The foundational elements of FlexRAID are shared physical resource pools called disk groups. Disk groups are comprised of physical drives of the same technology and performance characteristics. A disk group can contain a maximum of 48 drives. Multiple disk groups can be created on the system. Disks of different sizes can be added into the same disk group if they are one size apart from each other (i.e. a disk group can be comprised of 7.68 TB and 15.36 TB drives but not 3.84 TB and 15.36 TB drives).

    In FlexRAID, RAID protection is assigned at the disk group level. FlexRAID supports the following RAID protection schemes:

    A disk group can have only one RAID protection scheme assigned to it. Disk groups are broken down into smaller groupings of drives called RAID clusters. A disk group can contain multiple RAID clusters which inherit the attributes of the parent disk group such as its RAID protection scheme. The number of drives in each RAID cluster is called the RAID width and this is determined by its RAID protection scheme. A cluster using RAID 5 8+1 protection will have a RAID width of 9 disks (data disks + parity disks). The host presentable namespaces/volumes are carved from the capacity contained within a RAID cluster.

    Single Drive Adds

    The physical location within the DMEs of the RAID cluster is determined by PowerMaxOS to ensure the highest fault tolerance, accessibility to the nodes, and available capacity utilization. This capability allows for single drive additions into a disk group rather than an entire RAID width as with the previous generations. This automatic configuration by PowerMaxOS means that a customer never needs to predetermine the physical layout of the drives in the system to achieve the highest levels of fault tolerance and performance. As drives are added into the system, PowerMaxOS automatically selects which disk group and RAID cluster the additional capacity will be allocated to.

    Faster Rebuild Times

    In the next generation PowerMax, disk groups can span across multiple DMEs in the system. A key enabler for FlexRAID disk groups to spanning multiple DMEs is the Dynamic Fabric. As stated earlier in this paper, the dynamic fabric treats the physical drives as a unique endpoint on a fabric allowing for any physical drive in the disk group to be accessed by any node in the system in a distributed, balanced manner regardless of which DME the drive is located in. This model also allows for rebuild operation of any drive to be distributed across all the nodes in the system. Being able to access the full computing power of all the nodes allows the system to improve rebuild efficiency by over 2x when compared to the previous generation PowerMax as 1 TB can be rebuilt in less than 10 minutes using the FlexRAID model.

    Flexible RAID architecture

    Efficient Sparing

    FlexRAID employes a distributed universal sparing algorithm where a fixed amount of drive capacity is reserved for sparing operations on a set of drives in the disk group. Spare capacity is distributed as slices (hypers) across the drives in a disk group, eliminating the need for idle dedicated spare drives in the system, and enabling all the drives in the system to participate in I/O operations. This capability allows sparing for up to the maximum of 48 disks in a disk group using the capacity of just one spare drive. Only when the system exceeds 48 disks will an additional spare drive be required.

    In summary, the combination of FlexRAID with the dynamic fabric allows for the following benefits over previous generation PowerMax systems:

    • More capacity using fewer drives: FlexRAID uses a universal sparing algorithm in which spare space is distributed across all the drives in a disk group, eliminating the need for an idle dedicated spare drive.
    • Flexible upgrades: Flexible RAID allows customers to add capacity to the system in single drive increments as the individual drives are treated as unique endpoints on the dynamic fabric. The system supports mixed drive sizes, allowing you to expand your storage capacity as needed. In any configuration, capacity upgrades can contain a maximum of two different underlying drive sizes to achieve the best useful capacity desired. This is automatically optimized by the configuration tools.   
    • Higher resilience with faster rebuilds: With Flexible RAID, drive rebuilds occur 2x faster. This is because of the distributed nature of the dynamic fabric allows for all drives to be accessed by all the nodes in the system. This allows for the rebuild process to be spread across all the compute resources in the system, increasing the computing power, which allows for increased parallel processing and concurrent execution of the rebuild tasks.

Glossary of Terms

  • This document uses the following PowerMax terminology:

    Terminology

    Terminology

    Equivalent term

    Definition

    Dell PowerMax 2500

    PowerMax 2500

    PowerMax 2500 is the second-generation entry level NVMe scale-out offering for the PowerMax family. It is designed to provide customers with a small ultra-dense storage footprint (4 PBe in only 5U)

    Dell PowerMax 8500

    PowerMax 8500

    PowerMax 8500 is the second-generation flagship NVMe scale-out offering of the PowerMax family. It features a true disaggregated storage architecture which can deliver up to 18 PBe of capacity to customers.

    Dell PowerMax family

    PowerMax

    The PowerMax family refers to the Dell NVMe-based, mission-critical data storage offering. The family includes the first-generation offerings PowerMax 2000 and 8000- and next-generation offerings PowerMax 2500 and 8500

    Disk group

    Disk group

    A shared physical resource pool of physical drives of the same technology, size, and performance characteristics. The drives inside the disk group pools are dived into subgroups called clusters. Disk Groups are a foundation level component of FlexRAID.

    Disaggregated Storage Architecture

    Disaggregated Storage

    Disaggregated storage decouples a storage array’s compute and storage components so they can be scaled and provisioned separately.

    Dynamic Media Enclosure

    DME

    DME refers to the NVMe-oF attached enclosures which house the physical storage drives of the system. All DMEs in the system can be accessed by all compute nodes via internal NVMe-oF SAN topologies.

    Dynamic Random-Access Memory

    DRAM

    Dynamic random-access memory (dynamic RAM or DRAM) is a type of random-access semiconductor memory that stores each bit of data in a memory cell, usually consisting of a tiny capacitor and a transistor, both typically based on metal-oxide-semiconductor (MOS) technology. DRAM is the highest performing storage medium but also the costliest from a $/GB perspective. DRAM must be continuously supplied with power and periodically rewritten to retain data

    Effective capacity (in Terabytes)

    TBe

    This capacity measurement includes the benefits of thin provisioning, inline compression, deduplication, and space-efficient copies.

    Endpoint

    Endpoint

    A point on a fabric in which an initiator or receiver can be attached

    Flexible RAID

    FlexRAID

    A RAID distribution model enabled by the disaggregation of compute and storage in the PowerMax system. It provides active/active RAID protection across storage pools in the system DMEs

    Global Cache

    Global Cache

    The global cache is the total size of user accessible memory across all PowerMax Nodes. This is pooled resource which is accessible by all nodes in the PowerMax system by using Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA)

    Hybrid memory, message-based fabric

    NVMe/RDMA

    NVMe/RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) is considered the highest performing of the NVMe-oF transport types because applications can access remote memory without the involvement of the host operating system or the network software stack. It can transfer data directly without involving the kernel and does not consume additional CPU cycles to process traffic. NVMe over InfiniBand (NVMe/IB) and NVMe/RDMA over Converged Ethernet (NVMe/RoCE) are examples of hybrid fabrics

    Memory based fabric

    Memory based fabric

    In memory-based fabrics, NVMe commands, responses, and data use shared memory between the host and storage subsystem. This method was primarily specified in the original NVMe base standard, which defined how NVMe commands and responses are mapped to the queues in shared memory in a host over the PCIe interface. This method is known as a memory-based transport mode. Its commands, responses, and data are transferred between host memory and storage by performing explicit memory read and write operations using Direct Memory Access (DMA) over the internal high-speed PCIe fabric. The NVMe/PCIe transport specification defines and describes the mechanisms for how this process is accomplished.

    Message based fabrics

    Message based fabrics

    In message-based fabrics, NVMe commands, responses, and data are encapsulated and placed into fabric-dependent packets for transmission over distance to a remote storage subsystem. NVMe/TCP and NVMe/FC are examples of message-based fabrics

    Node

    Node

    Contains the compute elements of the next generation PowerMax storage system – CPU, memory, and I/O modules. Roughly equivalent to a first generation PowerMax director

    Node Pair

    Node Pair

    Two PowerMax nodes – roughly equivalent to a first generation PowerMax engine.

    Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe)

    NVMe

    NVMe is a command set and its associated storage-interface standards that specify efficient access to data storage devices and systems based on Non-Volatile Memory (NVM).

    NVMe Namespace

    Namespace

    Namespace is a generic term that refers to a contiguous area of storage that the host can access directly. It represents the mapping of the associated nonvolatile memory to a formatted logical block address (LBA) range. An NVMe namespace is equivalent to a SCSI logical unit (LU) or volume.

    NVMe over Fabric

    NVMe-oF

    NVM Express over Fabrics (NVMe-oF) defines a common architecture that supports a range of memory and message-based fabrics for the transport of NVMe data and commands.

    NVMe over Fibre Channel

    NVMe/FC

    NVMe/FC is an extension of the NVMe base specification that defines the binding of the NVMe protocol to message-based fabrics using the Fibre Channel Transport Protocol. NVMe/FC is an example of a message-based fabric.

    NVMe over PCIe

    NVMe/PCIe

    NVMe/PCIe is an extension of the NVMe base specification that defines the binding of the NVMe protocol to memory-based fabrics using Peripheral Component Interface Express (PCIe).

    NVMe over InfiniBand

    NVMe/IB

    NVMe/IB is an extension of the NVMe base specification that defines the binding of the NVMe protocol to hybrid memory, message-based fabrics using Ethernet and the InfiniBand transport protocol. NVMe/IB is an example of a hybrid memory, message based (NVMe/RDMA) fabric

    NVMe over TCP

    NVMe/TCP

    NVMe/TCP is an extension of the NVMe base specification that defines the binding of the NVMe protocol to message-based fabrics using Ethernet and the Transport Control Protocol (TCP). NVMe/TCP is an example of a message-based fabric

    Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe)

    PCIe

    A high-performance peripheral I/O bus architecture employed in enterprise servers, storage devices, cloud computing equipment, PCs, mobile devices, industrial computing, and automation systems, and Internet of Things (IoT) applications. It is not an overstatement when said that our modern interconnected world would not exist if not for PCIe.

    PCIe Switched Fabric

    PCIe Fabric

    A switched fabric architecture that uses PCIe switches to connect the PCIe root to various PCIe endpoints

    Persistent Memory

    PMEM

    A type of memory, also referred to as “storage class memory”, which combines the durability of flash storage while approaching the performance characteristics of more expensive DRAM. It does not use electrons to store information, instead it uses heat to change the state of the cell, from amorphous to crystalline, changing the resistance of the cell. By doing this, PMEM can retain its data even after the power is off.

    PowerMaxOS 10 

     

    PowerMaxOS 10

    The PowerMaxOS 10 release is the primary storage software which manages the next generation PowerMax systems – the PowerMax 2500 and PowerMax 8500. It cannot be installed on previous generation PowerMax or VMAX systems

    Root Complex

    PCIe Root or Root

    The primary connection mechanism which connects the CPU(s) and memory to the PCIe switched fabric.

    Scale out

    Scale out

    Scale out refers to adding compute nodes to grow performance

    Scale up

    Scale up

    Scale up refers to adding additional capacity to the PowerMax storage pools

    Storage Resource Pool

    SRP

    A Storage Resource Pool (SRP) is a collection of physical disks which constitute a specific usable capacity for customer application data. Most PowerMax arrays consist of a single SRP. An SRP's usable capacity can be comprised of Automated Data Placement across the SCM and NAND Flash drives within the SRP is managed by the internal PowerMax machine learning engine. Each SRP is protected by a single RAID protection scheme and can provide capacity for FBA, file and Mainframe.

    Unisphere™ for PowerMax

    Unisphere

    Unisphere for PowerMax is a graphical user interface that enables management and monitoring of both first and next generation PowerMax arrays along with legacy VMAX All Flash, VMAX3™, and VMAX 1 or 2 arrays. Unisphere for PowerMax also provides REST API interface for managing and controlling the storage system.

    Usable capacity (in Terabytes)

    TBu

    This refers to the amount of physical drive capacity available in the array, considering the RAID efficiency of the RAID type in use.

Highly Efficient and Performant Backup Processes

  • Efficiency is also a hallmark of Storage Direct Protection. The system employs an incremental-forever backup methodology, capturing only the changes since the last backup. This optimization conserves both bandwidth and storage. Furthermore, PowerProtect processes only unique blocks, achieving an outstanding data reduction ratio of up to 65:1, which minimizes network load.

    Storage Direct Protection enhances backup efficiency:

    • Incremental Forever Backups: Backups are conducted using an incremental-forever methodology, capturing only changes since the last backup. This approach conserves bandwidth and storage.
    • Unique Block Transfers: PowerProtect processes only unique blocks, achieving an impressive data reduction ratio of up to 65:1, minimizing network load.

    The performance specifications linked to Storage Direct Protection are noteworthy as well. Utilizing PowerMax’s Data Mover, the integration can achieve backup speeds of up to 46TB per hour, facilitating quick completion of backup tasks. In terms of recovery, the system excels with restore speeds of up to 21TB per hour, ensuring rapid access to critical data.

    The performance specifications associated with Storage Direct Protection are noteworthy:

    • Backup Speed: With PowerMax’s Data Mover, backups can achieve speeds up to 46TB per hour, enabling quick completion of backup tasks.
    • Restore Speed: Recovery operations can restore data at speeds of up to 21TB per hour, ensuring quick re-access to critical data.

    Storage Direct Protection – Efficient and Performant Backups and Restores

    Storage Direct Protection offers robust restore capabilities, providing multiple recovery options:

    • Restore to Original Storage Group: Administrators can restore data directly back to the original storage group on PowerMax.
    • New Volume Restoration: Data can be restored to new volumes within the same source array, offering more flexibility in data management.
    • Cross-Array Recovery: Organizations can restore data to storage groups on different PowerMax arrays, enabling comprehensive data recovery strategies.
    • Instant Access: This feature allows administrators to mount a copy of the storage group for surgical recovery, facilitating precise data retrieval as needed.

Host Connectivity Options

  • The combination of the next generation PowerMax hardware architecture and PowerMaxOS provides customers with the industry’s most diverse set of host connectivity options. Both the PowerMax 2500 and 8500 are the only enterprise level storage arrays which can support open systems block, file, and mainframe workload I/O within a single system.

    The PowerMax node pair enclosure features support for up to eight 2nd generation I/O modules (4 per node and 8 per node pair) allowing for up to 16 I/O ports per node (up to 32 ports per node pair). The PowerMax 2500 can scale to 64 host ports per system while the PowerMax 8500 can scale to 256 host ports per system. These hot swappable I/O modules provide a high-speed, low latency I/O connection between customer host environments and the PowerMax compute nodes. The I/O modules connect into the enclosure mid plane using a 16 lane (x16) PCIe connections.

    Typical PowerMax 2nd Generation four port I/O Module

    Prior generations of PowerMax required different I/O modules for the various protocols being supported. The 2nd Generation I/O modules have been redesigned to support multiple fabric transport types and protocols on a single four and two port cards. The table below details the I/O module card type, and their supported protocols used in both the PowerMax 2500 and PowerMax 8500:

    As stated earlier, all PowerMax I/O modules are hot swappable components. On top of this, each port on the I/O module can be individually controlled by management software such as Unisphere, where each port can be turned on or off by an authorized user. The individual optics used by each are also hot swappable. The I/O modules will each typically consume around 35 Watts of Power.

    Converged Emulations

    The next generation I/O module supports a new concept introduced in PowerMaxOS 10 called Converged Emulations. An emulation in PowerMax is also referred to as a “slice”. Each node supports 4 slices. In the PowerMax 2500 and 8500 the slice types are shown in the following table:

    PowerMax Slice and Corresponding Emulation Types

    Slice Type

    Use Case

    Slice A: (EM)

    Used for the Infrastructure Management  (EM) emulation

    Slice B: (DN)

    Used for backend services (DN)

    Slice C: (OR)1

    The converged emulation (OR) can be used for:

    Fibre Channel SCSI

    NVMe/TCP

    iSCSI

    GbE SRDF

    SRDF over Fibre Channel

    NVMe/FC

     

    Slice D: (EF)

    The Mainframe emulation. (EF) emulation is used for mainframe:

    FICON

    zHyperlink Mainframe (zHL)

    The converged emulation slice type of “OR” replaces the previous generation PowerMax FA, SE, RE, FN, RF emulations. The OR slice also allows for the intermixing of different transport protocols on the same I/O module. For example, on an Ethernet fabric I/O module, two ports could be used for NVMe/TCP, another for iSCSI, and the other for GbE SRDF.

    Understanding PowerMax Port Identities (ID)

    PowerMaxOS assigns both physical and logical identifiers (ID) to the next generation PowerMax I/O modules and ports. PowerMaxOS assigns a physical port ID to a port to designate its actual physical location in the array (node, slot, and port number) and the specific underlying fabric type it supports (Fibre Channel, Ethernet). The physical port information is most often used internally by PowerMaxOS and by Dell customer support personnel for troubleshooting purposes such as running low level inline commands on the array.

    PowerMaxOS also assigns a logical port ID to the physical ports on the systems.               The logical port ID is what customers use for storage provisioning through the array management tools such as Unisphere, Solutions Enabler, and RESTAPI.

    PowerMax Logical Port Number Scheme

    A total of 16 logical ports (0-0xF hexadecimal) are supported per node as shown in the above image. Logical Ports are displayed using the following nomenclature: <Emulation Type>-<Node number><Slice number>:<logical port number>. Here are some examples:

    • OR-1C:3 (Emulation Type: OR, Node 1, Slice C which is the OR emulation, logical port 3). This would correspond to the lower port in node 1 slot 1 in the  above figure.
    • OR-2C:7 (Emulation Type: OR, Node 2, Slice C, logical port 7). This would correspond to the upper most port in node 2 slot 2 in the above figure

    Logical port numberings in the Unisphere’s SystemàHardware view

    With converged emulation technology, the transport protocol assignments assigned to a logical port are dynamic and can be managed and changed by the user by using Unisphere for PowerMax, Solutions Enabler, or RESTAPI. For example, the protocol of a logical port OR-1C:0 in the above image, which is currently configured to support FC-SCSI, could be changed to FC-SRDF by selecting the port, placing it offline, and then selecting the Manage Protocol button.

    Note: Transport protocols used by the converged emulation must be supported by the hardware of the port. The APIs, CLI and UI give the users filter options so that they can easily identify the protocols supported by the underlying hardware.

    The following bullets provide additional useful information about the PowerMax logical port numbering scheme and how it is used:

    • Both PowerMax 2500 and 8500 use the same logical port numbering scheme
    • Node port labeling is inverted between nodes
    • If I/O module slots are not present, those port numbers are not used.
    • If I/O modules with two ports are present, the lower two ports for that I/O module slot are used. This is the case with the two port 100 GbE I/O modules.
    • The port number will always be in the same physical location for any given emulation or I/O module

Identification and protection

  • The best cyber security strategies begin with prevention and the PowerMax is purpose-built to prevent unauthorized access to system resources. Each model incorporates intrinsic security features and comprehensive access controls to safeguard company data. These features include:

    • Hardware root of trust (HWRoT) represents the foundation on which all secure operations of PowerMax depend. HWRoT contains the keys used for cryptographic functions and enables a secure boot process, preventing system boot if firmware is tampered with.
    • Firmware updates require a digital signature before updates can be applied.
    • Hardware-based data encryption through FIPS 140-2 level 2 certified self-encrypting drives (SEDs) ensures protection in case a drive is removed from the system.
    • Secure access controls and tamper proof audit logs protect from unauthorized access through secure logs of all events on PowerMax.
    • Multi-factor authentication for Admin Access (MFA) provides 2-factor authentication to management access using RSA SecureID.

Improved Security

  • PowerMax AIOps provides real-time visibility into incoming data characteristics, analyzing I/O patterns and data reduction rates, then comparing them to historical patterns. PowerMax AIOps algorithms can identify unusual patterns and anomalies that may indicate a security breach. This real-time visibility enables IT teams to respond quickly to potential threats, minimizing the risk of data loss or other security breaches. This capability is discussed more in the next section.

    PowerMax Cybersecurity

    Data is the life blood of the modern connected world. Cyber-attacks and breeches in which data is stolen, altered, and rendered unusable can cost corporations many millions of dollars in lost revenue. The next generation PowerMax systems have been designed to provide our customers nothing less than the highest levels of data protection and cyber security in the industry by fully implementing the Dell Cybersecurity Model. The Dell cybersecurity model aligns with the National Institute of Standards and Technologies (NIST) cybersecurity framework and is centered on the following principles: identification and protection; detection and response; recovery.

Issue Resolution and Remediation

  • Issue resolution and remediation are two distinct concepts that are often used interchangeably, but they serve different purposes in the process of addressing problems. Issue resolution focuses on identifying the root cause of a problem and finding a temporary solution to fix the symptoms, whereas remediation involves permanently correcting the underlying cause of the issue to prevent its recurrence. Both are crucial: issue resolution provides immediate relief, while remediation ensures long-term stability. Effective issue resolution can lead to temporary fixes, but remediation ensures that the problem is truly addressed, reducing the likelihood of future occurrences.

    PowerMax AIOps leverages advanced artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms which provide both issue resolution and remediation capabilities, enabling IT teams to quickly identify and respond to issues before they impact business operations. With its unique ability to analyze vast amounts of data and automate root cause analysis, PowerMax AIOps resolves issues faster and more accurately, reducing mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to resolve (MTTR). Moreover, its proactive remediation capabilities enable organizations to proactively fix underlying causes, preventing issues from recurring, and ensuring long-term stability and reliability of IT systems.

    An example of this, PowerMax AIOPs provides significant enhancements by enabling the SRDF Reporting and Remediations Solution. This solution greatly improves the way organizations manage their replication environments by maintaining consistent replication, reducing troubleshooting time, and improving overall resource utilization.

    SRDF State Status display in PowerMax for Unisphere

    The SRDF Reporting and Remediations Solution provides the following key functionality:

    • Reduce SRDF troubleshooting and triage time via built in recommendations and remediations to maintain healthy status.
    • Simplify planning and sizing for new and existing workloads to maintain healthy resource utilization across array nodes, host fabrics, and replication network bandwidth.
    • Improve SRDF/A restart automation to recover dropped replication sessions without requiring manual intervention.

    Aside from providing improvements SRDF, PowerMax AIOps provides other resolution and remediation capabilities for:

    PowerMax AIOps Remediations

    Remediation Type

    AIOPs Description

    Potential Remediation Examples

    Remediations for effective capacity breaches

    Algorithm predicts max capacity threshold breaches with in CloudIQ and sends space reclaim recommendations in the form of job lists to Unisphere

    •         Identify reclaimable SG space (ie inactive SG’s, no masking views)

    •         Provide data reduction assessment for SG’s with DRR disabled.

    •         Snap space cleanup for old, orphaned snaps.

    •         Recommend migration workload to other arrays with space

    Remediations for performance SLO breaches

    Algorithm runs through Root Cause Analysis (RCA) engine to identify cause of performance issue and recommended fixes and sends remediations to Unisphere

    •         Array/SG performance congestions due to “noisy neighbors”.

    •         Array/Node front end IO port congestion.

    •         Fabric pathing across too Few Ports/paths

    •         Fabric SFP port issues and stability

    Remediations for vWitness config issues

    Algorithms assesses the setup and status and sends remediation to Unisphere

    •         Monitor initial setup to validate successful configuration.

    •         Monitor status and alert if changes are made and how to fix issues

    Proactive monitoring and remediations for SFP predicted failures

    Algorithms monitor fabric Tx/Rx Light Levels and Failure (FPIN) data and provides single port and batch fabric predictions to Unisphere

    •         Add additional Array FE port to increase fabric resiliency.

    •         Identify bad/flaky SFP’s to be proactively serviced or replaced

    Dell AIOps Assistant

    Customers using PowerMax now have the distinct advantage of engaging in insightful dialogues with the Dell AIOps Assistant. This artificial intelligence-based tool is a natural language model that has been specifically customized using a vast array of Dell Engineering materials.

    The Dell AIOps Assistant's training foundation lies in its extensive database of over 133,000 Knowledge Base articles, white papers, blogs, and other robust content sources. Besides PowerMax, the Assistant is also equipped to handle queries and provide information about every Dell infrastructure product—ranging from servers to switches—thereby offering a comprehensive, one-stop solution for all Dell-related inquiries and issues.

    Dell AIOps Assistant Overview

    The AIOps assistant allows customers to engage in natural conversations and ask it follow-up questions to understand issues in more detail – just like other AI language models used on the web such as ChatGPT or Co-Pilot. To illustrate, a user could instruct the assistant to "outline the procedure for a PowerMaxOS 10 upgrade." This simple request leverages the power of natural language processing to not only provide a comprehensible response but also deliver the corresponding documentation for further reference. This capability will potentially save customers hours of research and resolve their questions and issues faster on their own, without having to call specialists or Dell Customer Support.

Local replication with TimeFinder SnapVX

  • PowerMax arrays come provide local replication data service with TimeFinder SnapVX.  SnapVX creates very low-impact snapshots. SnapVX supports up to 256 snapshots per source volume, up to 1024 snapshots per source using Snapshot Policies or zDP, and up to 65 million total snapshots per array. Users can assign names to identify their snapshots, and they can set automatic expiration dates on each snapshot.

    SnapVX provides the ability to manage consistent point-in-time copies for storage groups with a single operation. Up to 1024 target volumes can be linked per source volume, providing read/write access as pointers or full-copy clones.

    Local replication with SnapVX creates pointer-based snapshots that preserves a point-in-time view of a source volume. Snapshots do not require additional volumes to work making them incredibly lightweight to get started. Snapshots share back-end allocations with the source volume and other snapshots of the source volume, and only consume additional space when the source volume is changed.

    Each snapshot has a user-defined name and can optionally have an expiration date, both of which can be modified later. Management interfaces provide the user with the ability to take a snapshot of an entire storage group with a single command.

    A point-in-time snapshot can be accessed from a host by linking it to a host-accessible volume referred to as a target. Target volumes are simply regular volumes that have been linked to a snapshot. Up to 1024 target volumes can be linked to the snapshot(s) of a single source volume. This limit can be achieved either by linking all 1024 target volumes to the same snapshot from the source volume, or by linking multiple target volumes to multiple snapshots from the same source volume. However, a target volume may only be linked to a single snapshot at a time. When snapshots are linked, the snapshot data is always preserved, any writes to the target volume are written to non-shared tracks on the storage resource pool, at any time the snapshots can be re-linked to the same set of devices or to another set of devices presenting the original point in time copy. This is especially useful when testing as the dataset can be restored to its original state instantly as the relink switches back to the preserved image of the snapshot and discards any non-shared tracks from previous test cycles.

    By default, targets are linked in a no-copy mode. This no-copy linked target functionality greatly reduces the number of writes to the back-end flash drives as it eliminates the requirement of performing a full volume copy of the source volume during the unlink operation to continue to use the target volume for host I/O. This saves the back-end flash devices from enduring a large amount of write activity during the unlink operation, further reducing potential write amplification on the PowerMax array.

Next Generation PowerMax Architecture

  • The next generation PowerMax systems are built from the same core design principles which has made the first generation PowerMax systems the go to storage platform for mission critical applications in the enterprise data center; however, where the second-generation platform architecture represents a significant departure from the first generation is in its efficiency and scalability.

    The next generation PowerMax systems employ new designs for the compute modules, midplanes, power supplies, fans, and system enclosures. The platform also adds the new functionality of an internal Data Processing Unit (DPU) which performs all data reduction and SRDF compression tasks. The primary components about the next generation PowerMax platform are:

Nodes contain the primary compute elements (CPU and memory) of the next generation systems. Each next generation PowerMax system has at least two nodes (a “node pair”).

Node Pairs and the Node Pair Enclosure

  • All next generation PowerMax systems use a minimum of two nodes. These are referred to as being a “Node Pair”. A node pair is roughly analogous to the previous generation PowerMax “engine”. Node Pairs are enclosed in their own 3U enclosure. Aside from the node pair, the node enclosure houses the enclosure mid-plane, up to 8 I/O modules (4 for each node), Fabric Attach Modules (FAM), Back-End Module (BEM) on PowerMax 2500 only, Four 1800-Watt Power Supplies, up to four 700-Watt Lithium-ION battery backup packs, plus Control Stations (CS) and Management Switch Modules (MSM).


    Node Connections to Enclosure Mid Plane

    The node pair enclosure midplane is the primary communication interface between the nodes, the I/O modules, control stations (CS), and management switch modules (MSM). This midplane is designed specifically for the PowerMax next generation architecture. The mid plane uses high bandwidth PCIe connections which allow for high data transfer rates while minimizing signal noise along the PCIe system bus. Internode communication occurs within the midplane using two PCIe x16 Compute Module Interconnect links (CMI 1 and CMI 2). All I/O modules, FAMs, BEMs, CSs, and MSMs attach to the enclosure midplane. All these attached components are hot swappable. The system power supplies also connect to the enclosure midplane making it the primary distributor of power within the system.

    Both nodes and all enclosure components, excluding the enclosure midplane, are hot swappable. The images below show the PowerMax Node Pairs as viewed from the front and back. The upper section (2U) of the enclosure houses the nodes in the front and the I/O modules, FAM and BEM modules in the rear. The lower section(1U) contains the control stations and battery backup modules in the front, with the system power supplies and management switch modules in the rear.

    PowerMax Node Pair Enclosure (Front)

    PowerMax 2500 Node Pair Enclosure (Rear)

    PowerMax 8500 Node Pair Enclosure (Rear)

    High Performance Cluster (HPC) Architecture

    Along with the dynamic fabric and Dynamic Media Enclosure (DME), both discussed later in this document, node pairs provide the bed rock of what makes the next generation PowerMax a truly active/active High-Performance Cluster (HPC) for storage. Active/Active means that both nodes are online at the same time processing host I/O and sharing the same pooled resources.

    Each is its own physical failure domain with its own power supplies and backup batteries. Each node can also access all the storage drives in the system using the dynamic fabric. If a failure occurs in one node, there is no need to engage any failover activities as I/O from the hosts to the storage devices will simply continue through the other non-failed node without interruption - assuming hosts are configured with redundant paths and multipathing software has been configured.

    In general, the next generation PowerMax cluster architecture provides the following benefits natively without the need for added hardware, software, or licensing costs:

    • High reliability and fault tolerance: All the nodes in the PowerMax can access application IO and supply resources to process it making it a true shared everything active/active system. In case of a node failure there is no failover operation needed as with active/passive systems as the next generation PowerMax system software (PowerMaxOS 10) will automatically redirect the failed nodes IO to other nodes. Since no failover is required, there is no need to ever configure a quorum device to guard against issues such as “split brain”.
    • Simplicity: The next generation PowerMax system appears to the user as a single entity. A user does not have to log into separate individual nodes to manage or configure the PowerMax system. The management of the entire system is performed using the HTML5-based Unisphere for PowerMax’s GUI and/or RESTAPI. These tools provide an easy-to-use interface for management actions and monitoring operations which are crucial to an organization’s needs.
    • Fully autonomous operations: PowerMaxOS 10 manages all system resources autonomously - continuously running diagnostics, scrubbing, and moving data within the system for maximum performance and availability 24x7. There is no need to manually configure load balancing between the nodes as PowerMaxOS 10 automatically decides which node will process the incoming IO data based on locality and resource availability.
    • Predicable performance and scalability: As compute requirements increase, the PowerMax can “scale out” by adding nodes pairs into the system non disruptively to supply a predictable linear increase in performance and computing power. As capacity requirements increase, the system can “scale up” in a granular manner using single drive increments. This allows PowerMax to scale based on application requirements rather than system architectural requirements. The architecture also enables holistic software scalability as the PowerMax can support 64K host presentable devices, over 65 million snapshots, and 2048 remote replication groups with other systems.

    Hardware Management Modules

    The next generation PowerMax management and monitoring solution was completely redesigned to provide improved performance and resiliency for monitoring and management operations. This solution is comprised of two separate hardware components: the Control Station (CS) and Management Switch Module (MSM). These two components replace the Management Module Control Station (MMCS) used in the previous generation PowerMax.

    The Control Station (CS)

    The CS module is a small blade server which uses Intel’s four core Denverton System on a Chip (SOC) hardware. The CS provides the computing power required to run the many internal system software programs that provide low level control, monitoring, and management used by internal Dell field and remote support personnel. Each next generation PowerMax node pair uses two CS modules (one for each node). The CS modules provide active/active redundancy for all critical system management, monitoring, and reporting functions. In the event of a single CS module failure, the system does not require automatic failover to the secondary CS module, as both modules provide continuous operation of these critical system functions. This redundant active/active approach ensures that customers and Dell support staff have continuous access to system, eliminating the possibility of “blind spots” where they are unable to access the system while waiting for a failover operation to complete.

    The CS modules are located on the front panel in the bottom U of the node pair enclosure. Both plug directly into the enclosure midplane and are hot swappable. The CS modules communicate with each other through the midplane via internal 10 GbE connections. The front of the CS module includes an RJ45 port for onsite Dell support staff to access the system for configuration and troubleshooting. Also included are two USB ports and a uHDMI port for connecting a keyboard, mouse, and monitor.

     Control Station Module

    The Management Switch Module (MSM)

    The second component of the next generation PowerMax management solution is the Management Switch Module (MSM). The MSM is a hot swappable four RJ45 port Ethernet switch module which manages all in bound and out bound external management communication to the node. Each node has its own dedicated MSM and each MSM plugs directly into chassis midplane. The node MSMs can be found in the back of the node pair enclosure in the bottom U of the 3U chassis. 

    Management Switch Module (MSM)

    • Port 1 on the MSM is dedicated as a connection point for Dell’s Secure Connect Gateway (SCG) for secure remote customer service access to the system.
    •  Port 2 on the MSM is dedicated as a connection point into the customer’s management/monitoring network. This port is the primary access point a customer will use to access the GuestOS containers such as the embedded Unisphere instance (PowerMaxOS and the GuestOS will be discussed in further detail in the next section). System SNMP alerts can be configured to be sent out through port 1 to Dell customer support and through port 2, to the customer’s internal management network. 
    • Ports 3 and 4 on the MSM are dedicated for communication to other CS units belonging to other node pairs on the system. On a single node pair system, ports 3 and 4 are not used.

    Redesigning the PowerMax management solution from a single component to a two-component solution with a separate compute blade and a dedicated four port Ethernet switch provides customers several advantages in terms of scalability, flexibility, performance, and redundancy. These benefits are summarized below:

    • Increased Network Connectivity: By transitioning to a separate switch with four RJ45 ports, the management solution gains a considerable increase in network connectivity. This allows for more network interfaces to be used simultaneously, facilitating better segregation of traffic (e.g., management, monitoring, user access), enhanced throughput for management tasks, and dedicated network connections for remote out-of-band access.
    • Improved Performance: Separate components can be optimized for their specific roles, leading to performance improvements. The CS blade is focused on handling the compute requirements of the critical system management and monitoring software without being burdened by the processing of network traffic overhead. The MSM can focus solely on processing the network traffic to and from the system.
    • Improved Redundancy and Availability: With separate components, maintenance, repair, and upgrades are more straightforward. If a node’s MSM requires service or replacement, it can be attended to without disturbing the CS blade, and vice versa. This leads to less downtime for maintenance activities.

    In summary, the two-component next generation PowerMax management solution offers enhanced capabilities in terms of network connectivity, system performance, and reliability. Decoupling the compute and networking components provides a more versatile and robust approach to array management that can better meet the needs of demanding and evolving data center environments.

Overview

  • Introduced in 2018, the Dell EMC PowerMax family was the first Dell EMC hardware platform that used an end-to-end Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) architecture for customer data. These systems were the PowerMax 2000 and PowerMax 8000. These NVMe-based PowerMax systems were specifically created to unlock the bandwidth, IOPS, and latency performance benefits that NVM media offers to host based applications. They are unattainable using the previous generation of all-flash storage arrays.

    Upon their launch, the PowerMax 2000 and PowerMax 8000 were quickly adopted by enterprise customers to form the storage bedrock of their mission critical data centers. However, data center requirements are not stagnant. Storage infrastructures are constantly being tasked to meet the increasing demands by next generation data centers and mission critical applications. They are known to require more security, performance, and far greater power efficiencies. To meet these demands facing our customers, Dell Technologies introduced two new members into the PowerMax family – the PowerMax 2500 and 8500 in 2022. 

    The PowerMax 2500 and 8500 systems represent and are referred to as the next generation of the PowerMax Family. There are five principles which will be mentioned throughout this paper to describe the next generation PowerMax: scalability, flexibility, performance, efficiency, and resiliency. The next generation systems are specifically designed using these principles to provide a disaggregated, share everything solution to meet the ever-increasing levels of performance, storage density, and high security required by enterprise data centers and mission critical applications. The PowerMax 2500 and 8500 have been specifically architected to provide customers with:

    • Innovative architecture – a fully disaggregated storage architecture which allows customers to scale storage and compute independently, a new Flexible RAID scheme (FlexRAID), and a redesigned internal dynamic fabric using NVMe/PCIe and NVMe/IB (InfiniBand)
    • The world’s most secure storage platform – Incorporating security into the hardware with Hardware Root of Trust (HWRoT), Secure Boot, Self-Encrypting Drives, Anomaly detection, and other features.
    • A balance of performance and power efficiency – Improvements of up to 2.5x IOPS/watt, up to 5x the effective capacity/watt, and 14x effective capacity/rack unit when compared to the previous PowerMax generation.
    • Higher storage density – 7X more effective capacity than previous PowerMax generation with up to 4 PB, 32 front end ports in only 5U with PowerMax 2500 with capability to scale out to over 18 PB and 256 front end ports in PowerMax 8500
    • Improved data reduction capabilities – worlds only platform to offer mainframe storage compression with a 3:1 data reduction guarantee, while also guaranteeing a 5:1 data reduction for open systems
    • A comprehensive set of modern host connectivity options – the platform offers support for both native SCSI and NVMe workloads using 10, 25, and 100 Gb for Ethernet connectivity, along with 32 and 64 Gb for Fibre Channel connectivity.
    • Unprecedented single system workload consolidation – the next generation PowerMax can consolidate open system block and mainframe workloads, along with file services that feature a 64-bit containerized micro service architecture that supports up to 64 TB NFS and SMB file systems – all within a single 5U storage system.

    Aside from the above, the PowerMax 2500 and 8500 have over 200 other new features and functions over the previous generation. With their new architecture, features, and functions, the PowerMax 2500 and 8500 have been designed from the ground up to meet the demands of next generation data center and applications well into the late-2020s and beyond.

PowerMax AIOps Strategy

  • PowerMax AIOps addresses these challenges by automating routine tasks such as data monitoring, capacity planning, performance optimization, and incident management. The PowerMax AIOps strategy focuses on the following areas:

    • Enhanced Automation: PowerMax AIOps automates repetitive and error-prone tasks, allowing IT teams to focus on more strategic activities. This leads to improved productivity, efficiency, and a reduction in operational costs.
    • Proactive Issue Identification and Resolution: By analyzing real-time data and identifying patterns through advanced analytics, PowerMax AIOps can predict and mitigate potential issues before they impact operations. This proactive approach aids in making informed decisions by providing actionable insights. This ultimately minimizes downtime, better resource allocation, and enhanced system reliability of the storage infrastructure.
    • Scalability: PowerMax AIOps enables the management of large-scale, multi-petabyte storage environments more effectively. It supports dynamic capacity and workload management, which is essential for supporting digital transformation and innovation.
    • Improved Security: PowerMax AIOps helps in identifying and responding to security threats more quickly by analyzing data from various sources and detecting anomalies.

    The PowerMax approach to AIOps aims to transition from manual to automated remediations, leveraging predictive analytics and automated actions to reduce triage time, escalations, and potential outages. The goal is to extend self-management from merely describing issues to actively prescribing solutions, thereby improving efficiency and reducing the need for manual interventions.
