PowerMax Cyber Recovery Service

  • The PowerMax Cyber Recovery Service is consulting-led ransomware solution is a comprehensive, tailor-made approach designed to protect and enhance business operations. It sets up a separate and secure environment, referred to as a vault, that ensures an additional layer of safety for sensitive data. This vault is controlled through encrypted access to bolster security measures.

    The ransomware solution also features immutable snapshots. These are essentially fixed copies of data that can't be altered or deleted, allowing for swift data rebuilding and minimizing Recovery Time Objective (RTO). This attribute helps businesses bounce back from potential cyber-attacks more rapidly and efficiently.

    Moreover, the provided solution emphasizes data isolation and immutability. This strategy reduces exposure to potential threats and helps businesses meet their compliance targets by ensuring that stored data cannot be altered without authorization. All these features together create a strong and resilient defense against ransomware threats.

    The following diagram highlights the primary components of the PowerMax Cyber Recovery Solution:

    PowerMax Cyber Recovery Solution primary components

    There are 3 basic steps to the PowerMax cyber vault data protection operation:

    1. Production data is synced through an SRDF air gap, which the management server unlocks into the vault and replicated into the vault target storage. The air gap is then re-locked.
    2. A copy of that data is made. (Vault retention of this data is configurable for different timeframes.)
    3. The vault is locked to provide additional protection from accidental or intentional deletion.

    Recovering data quickly from the vault in the event of a cyber-attack (or simply for recovery testing procedures) is critical. Customers can use native PowerMax software (SnapVX, SRDF) to recover their data or work with Dell Professional Services.

    Note: For more detailed information about PowerMax’s Cybersecurity features, please consult the following white paper: https://infohub.delltechnologies.com/en-us/t/dell-powermax-cybersecurity-1/

    PowerMax Multicloud Mobility

    With the advent of PowerMaxOS 10.1 and enhancements introduced in version 10.2, Dell has launched a significant feature known as “Storage Direct Protection”. This native integration allows organizations to seamlessly back up their PowerMax storage directly to PowerProtect Data Domain (PPDD) appliances while ensuring zero performance impact on host applications. This section delves into the advantages and functionalities of this integration, particularly its flexibility, efficiency, and the comprehensive management capabilities provided by PowerProtect Data Manager (PPDM).

PowerMax Nodes

  • The PowerMax 2500 and PowerMax 8500 are built on 1U modular building blocks called “nodes”. Nodes contain the root complex including the primary compute elements (CPU and memory) of the second-generation systems. The Nodes are roughly analogous to the previous generation “director” component.

    The node is the primary compute building block of the next generation PowerMax system. All PowerMax nodes use a full width 1U form factor sled which plugs into the mid plane of the Node Pair Enclosure. PowerMax nodes are hot swappable.

    PowerMax Node (top view with lid off)

    PowerMax Node (front view)

    The following section details some of the core PowerMax node elements.

    Dual Intel Xeon Scalable CPUs

    The next-generation PowerMax node leverages dual multi-core Intel Scalable Xeon processors which presents a powerful value proposition for businesses and data centers that demand high-capacity, high-performance, and highly reliable storage infrastructure. These multi-core Xeon processors provide the vital computational strength necessary for the next generation PowerMax array to manage massive I/O operations with ease, a critical requirement for data-heavy environments. The parallel processing capabilities inherent in multi-core technology greatly enhance the efficiency of storage operations all while maintaining system performance.

    Each PowerMax node is dual socketed and uses the following Intel Scalable Xeon Processors:

    • PowerMax 2500 – Each CPU has 16 cores running at 2.8 GHz (32 cores total per node)
    • PowerMax 8500 – Each CPU has 18 cores running at 3.9 GHz (36 cores total per node)
    • Each CPU can consume up to 205 Watts / processor.

    Additionally, these processors feature extensive cache sizes and implement sophisticated technologies that fine-tune workload distribution and energy consumption, essential for ensuring continuous system reliability and for keeping operational expenditures in check. With such advanced processing power at its core, the next-generation PowerMax array is engineered to support the most demanding enterprise applications, ensuring data integrity, scalability, and performance continuity, all aligned with the future needs of data-driven organizations.

    Node Memory Configurations

    The next generation PowerMax systems feature multiple memory configurations which allows for increased workload density and capacity while reducing the overall system footprint. This results in higher efficiencies and lower costs.

    Each next generation PowerMax node features 24 DDR4 slots for a blend of Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM) and persistent memory (PMEM). This high number of memory slots allows the PowerMax to achieve an optimal balance of speed and capacity, utilizing DRAM for its ultra-fast read/write capabilities and PMEM memory for its durability and non-volatility.

    The platform generates a significant amount of dynamic and persistent metadata especially as the system scales out in capacity. In the previous generation this meta data was stored in expensive DRAM memory. However, the use of Persistent Memory (PMEM) in the next generation PowerMax systems eliminates the need for storing metadata in DRAM, greatly improving system efficiency and costs, especially as systems scale out to multiple petabytes.

    The use of PMEM also enables more efficient data vaulting. Since data in PMEM is persistent, it does not need to be vaulted during shutdowns or emergency procedures, reducing system demands and lowering the keep-alive time requirements for internal battery backup systems. This results in faster vaulting speeds and reduced power consumption.

    Furthermore, the use of PMEM in the system allows for the storage of more system metadata at a lower cost per gigabyte, enabling significant increases in storage capacity without adding significant cost. This results in a lower cost of ownership for PowerMax systems. Additionally, the reduced system keep-alive times enabled by PMEM allow for the use of smaller backup batteries, reducing the overall system footprint by 2U per node pair.

    Overall, the integration of PMEM in the next generation PowerMax systems offers numerous benefits, including improved efficiency, lower costs, and reduced system footprint. These advancements enable PowerMax systems to provide higher levels of performance, capacity, and reliability while reducing the total cost of ownership.

    Each node uses the 24 DDR4 DIMM slots reserved in the following manner:

    • 12 slots specified for DDR4 DRAM - providing up to a maximum of 768 GB of DRAM capacity per node (1.5 TB per node pair). The system DRAM is used for caching customer data and small amounts dynamic system meta data.
    • Up to 12 slots specified for Permanent Memory (PMEM) – providing over 3 TB of PMEM capacity per node (over 6 TB per node pair).

    The following table shows the supported node memory configurations and the max effective storage capacity that they support:

    Supported PowerMax memory configurations and associated effective capacities.

    Here are some important considerations regarding PowerMax memory configurations:

    • Memory configuration options are fixed. You cannot scale DRAM and PMEM independently.
    • Memory configuration 1 is supported only on the PowerMax 2500
    • Memory configuration 1 only supports an eMgmt guest. Memory configuration 2 or higher is required for the inclusion of all other guest types such as SDNAS and VASA, . (The guests will be discussed in more detail in the PowerMaxOS section of this paper)Node pairs can consist of nodes with different/intermixed memory configuration sizes, but they can only be one size difference apart (i.e. Node 1 uses configuration 1 while Node 2 uses configuration 2)

    Typical PowerMax DRAM (top) and PMEM (bottom) DIMMS

    In summary, the sophisticated memory architecture of the next generation PowerMax node is designed to meet the evolving needs of modern data centers, supporting rapid data access, and delivering cost-efficient capacity expansion capabilities.

    Internal 64 GB M.2 SSD boot drive

    The next generation PowerMax uses an M.2 SSD DIMM for a boot drive. This encapsulates a forward-thinking approach to infrastructure design, recognizing the critical nature of system availability, stability, and performance optimization in today's competitive and ever-accelerating data landscape. This small drive contains all the PowerMax OS 10 executables used by the system. The M.2 drive is mounted on its own 140 pin printed circuit board (PCB) riser and is situated in a x4 PCIe slot in the middle of the 24 DIMM slots.

    Internal M.2 Boot SSD on PCB riser card

    Internal Data Processing Unit (DPU)

    The next generation PowerMax uses an internal Data Processing Unit (DPU)  as standard for data reduction and Symmetrix Remote Data Facility (SRDF) encryption. This represents another forward-thinking design for several compelling reasons.

    • A DPU is a specialized processor designed to offload and accelerate specific data-centric tasks that would otherwise consume valuable CPU resources. By dedicating a DPU to handle data reduction—such as deduplication and compression—the PowerMax can optimize data footprint efficiency, enabling cost savings on storage space and improving overall system performance.
    • When it comes to SRDF encryption, incorporating the DPU ensures that data in transit between primary and secondary sites is protected without any performance overhead. This specialized hardware allows for seamless, uninterrupted data services with enterprise-grade encryption, providing robust data protection that meets stringent compliance and business continuity requirements.
    • Previous generation PowerMax 2000 and 8000 models require a front facing data reduction module. The use of an internal DPU eliminates the need for this front facing module which further reduces the overall system footprint.

    The use of internal DPUs gives PowerMax an architecture that is built to address the ever-increasing demands for data security and optimized storage management in a world where data is both an asset and a liability.

    Note: For more detail on the DPU used in PowerMax please visit the following blog: New PowerMax Architecture Adds NVIDIA BlueField DPU Technology

    A Platform Controller Hub (PCH)

    The Platform Controller Hub (PCH) at the heart of the next-generation PowerMax server architecture. It is a pivotal component that enhances both performance and reliability. Centralizing control over the systems integral functions, including PCIe for high-speed connectivity, internal M.2 boot drive, and SATA controllers for the front facing vault drives (Drive 0 and Drive 1) to which the system will write the contents of DRAM in the event of a total power loss. These drives are self-encrypting, so the data vaulted out of DRAM is FIPS 140-2 secure. The system meta data stored in PMEM is persistent, so it does not need to be vaulted. As said earlier, no user data is stored in PMEM.

    Note: For the PowerMax 2500 - only one vault drive per node is needed unless the maximum node DRAM configuration (768 GB) is used

    Additionally, the PCH orchestrates the Baseboard Management Controller (BMC), a subsystem critical for overseeing the node’s Enhanced Adaptive Cooling. Through precise regulation of fan operation and power distribution, the BMC ensures that the system operates within optimal temperature ranges and energy parameters, contributing to the sustainability of the system's performance and extending its longevity.

    Enhanced Adaptive Cooling

    The Next Generation PowerMax Systems incorporate intelligent Baseboard Management Controllers and variable speed fan technology to help drive thermal and power efficiency. Each next generation node uses four 40mm variable speed dual-fan modules that house 16 total fan rotors. In conjunction with the midplane venting and heatsink solutions, the fans provide cooling for the CPUs, DIMMs, I/O modules and a management switch module.

    The variable speed fans are designed to adjust their rotational speed based on the system's cooling requirements. Instead of running at a fixed speed, they dynamically adapt to the heat load generated by the components. This intelligent control enables precise temperature regulation and optimized cooling efficiency. By operating at lower speeds when the system is not under heavy load, variable speed fans reduce noise levels and power consumption. On the other hand, when the system experiences higher workloads, the fans automatically ramp up their speed to provide effective cooling, ensuring reliable performance under the most demanding conditions.

    The fans are controlled by an intelligent Baseboard Management Controller (BMC) module. The BMC acts as the central management hub for the system, offering enhanced monitoring and control capabilities. It provides real-time insights into the system's health, temperature, power consumption, and other vital parameters. The BMC constantly monitors the following node thermal parameters:

    • On-board Ambient temperature sensor located at the cooling fan exhaust. This provides the inlet temperature to the CPU Module prior to pre-heating of any components.
    • DIMM Thermal Sensor data – This data is collected by the CPU and is accessed by the BMC.
    • CPU Thermal Sensor data – This data is accessed via the Platform Environment Control Interface (PECI) on the CPU by the BMC
    • Power Supply temperature data – This data is accessed by the BMC over the Inter-Integrated bus (I2C).

    Using the previous internal and external ambient temperature values, the BMC will automatically adjust the fan speed using a fan control algorithm so that internal node temperatures are always within specified ranges.

    The combination of using intelligent BMC and variable speed fans provide numerous benefits in terms of system management and cooling efficiency for the next generation PowerMax platform. These benefits include:

    • Enhanced system monitoring and control: The BMC enables comprehensive monitoring of critical system parameters, facilitating proactive management and timely intervention when needed.
    • Increased operational efficiency: The BMC's proactive management and optimization capabilities contribute to improved overall system efficiency, leading to better resource utilization, and reduced operational costs.
    • Precise temperature regulation: Variable speed fans adapt their speed according to the system's cooling needs, maintaining optimal temperatures for the components and ensuring their longevity and performance.
    • Energy efficiency: Variable speed fans operate at lower speeds during periods of low system activity, reducing power consumption and minimizing energy waste. This not only saves costs but also contributes to a greener and more sustainable operation.

    In summary, an intelligent board management controller and variable speed fans offer system next generation PowerMax customers greater control, improved reliability, optimized cooling efficiency, and enhanced energy savings. These technologies play a crucial role in creating more efficient and sustainable storage environments for the modern data center.

    Note: For more specific information on the next generation PowerMax’s industry leading power efficiency and sustainability capabilities go to the following white paper:  The Next Generation PowerMax – A balance of performance at scale and power efficiency and the associated blog at: The Next Generation PowerMax: Performance with Efficiency and Sustainability Unleashed

    A Future Proof and Efficient PCIe Architecture

    A key design objective of the next generation PowerMax is to ensure that it’s PCIe architecture can provide customers with a future proof platform that would be able to meet the increasing enterprise storage demands for performance and efficiency well into the late 2020s, without requiring expensive hardware upgrades that feature faster CPUs and PCIe bus speeds. The PowerMax 2500 and 8500 architecture was designed with enough performance headroom to easily scale so that it could meet the additional application, and workload demands placed on it by customers over the expected lifespan of the systems.

    This future proof design provides a stable and reliable storage system that provides numerous advantages to customers such as:

    • Reduced Costs: Without the need for frequent hardware upgrades, customers can reduce their costs associated with hardware maintenance, upgrades, and replacement.
    • Increased Uptime: Customers can reduce the risk of downtime and ensure their systems remain available and operational, minimizing the impact on business operations.
    • Simplified Management: Customers can simplify management and maintenance, as administrators can focus on other critical tasks and reduce the complexity of managing multiple hardware upgrades
    • Improved Predictability: Customers can better predict and plan for their workload demands, allowing them to make informed decisions about capacity planning and resource allocation.
    • Reduced Complexity: Not having to frequently upgrade hardware will reduce the overall complexity of the storage infrastructure, making it easier to manage and maintain.
    • Improved Scalability: With a storage system that can scale to meet growing demands without requiring upgrades, customers can more easily adapt to changing business requirements and growth.
    • Enhanced Security: A stable and reliable storage system can provide a stronger foundation for security, as customers can focus on protecting their data and applications without worrying about frequent upgrades and potential vulnerabilities.
    • Better ROI: By reducing the need for frequent upgrades, customers can achieve a better return on investment (ROI) from their storage infrastructure, as they can allocate resources more efficiently and effectively.

    A key element of the next-generation PowerMax architecture was careful selection of the components involved in creating the underlying PCIe fabric. Each next-generation PowerMax node uses a new switched PCIe fabric which has been optimized for both efficiency and performance. Each node’s PCIe fabric uses a partitionable, multi-rooted, switched architecture. This architecture enables advanced PCIe functionality that increases system configurability, optimizes system resource utilization, and availability.

    The new architecture has allowed for replacing multiple discrete physical PCIe switches with a single partitioned switch. This shrinks the total cost of ownership by reducing power consumption, decreasing board space requirements, and lowering system interconnect costs. Additionally, the unified switch complex reduces system development costs through hardware reuse that enables a single hardware platform to serve many end markets and price/performance points. This is one of the key enablers which allows the reuse of the same node architecture in the both the PowerMax 2500 and PowerMax 8500.

    Using a multirooted partitionable PCIe architecture greatly enhances resiliency on the PowerMax. Resources associated with a failing node root are dynamically reassigned to operational roots. This architecture allows any number of the remaining functional roots to take control of the isolated system resources to reestablish service with no interruption and no data loss.

    In the Next Generation PowerMax there only three primary PCIe switches in each node:

    • 64 lane PCIe Switch A with a x16 connection to CPU1, x16 connection to the root complex of the peer node, x16 connections to I/O modules 0 and 1
    • 64 lane PCIe Switch B with a x16 connection to CPU2, x16 connection to the root complex of the peer node, x16 connections to I/O modules 2 and 3
    • 48 lane PCIe switch with a x16 connection to CPU 2, x16 connection to internal DPU, x4 connections to vault drives 0 and 1

    The 64 lane PCIe switches are partitioned in such a manner that there are dual x16 lane connections to the root complex of the peer node. Each node has PCIe access with the other nodes components such as its memory and I/O modules. This access allows for the augmenting of compute resources for a fixed set of I/O and peripherals. This provides an overall system performance boost by allowing additional compute resources from multiple nodes to help process I/O coming in from the hosts and going to the storage.

    High Level PowerMax Node PCIe Block Diagram

    The PCIe switches employ an intelligent port arbitration scheme that dynamically allocates the appropriate bandwidth and resources for unimpeded data transfer between the connected peripheral devices and the CPU along the PCIe fabric. This intelligent port allocation scheme allows the PCIe switches to do the following:

    • Efficient Resource Utilization: enables the dynamic allocation of resources such as bandwidth, power, and data paths based on the real-time requirements of connected devices. This efficient allocation ensures that resources are utilized optimally, maximizing the overall system performance.
    • Quality of Service (QoS): allows the switches to prioritize and allocate resources to critical devices or applications, ensuring that they receive the necessary bandwidth and latency requirements for optimal performance. This is particularly important in applications where consistent and predictable performance is essential, such as in high-performance computing or data center environments.
    • Flexibility and Scalability: The PCIe switches can adapt to changing usage patterns and requirements, dynamically adjusting resource allocation as needed. This flexibility is crucial in environments where the number and types of connected devices may vary, allowing for efficient utilization of the switch's capabilities.
    • Support for Diverse Workloads: By dynamically managing resource allocation, the PCIe switches can efficiently support diverse workloads, including a mix of low-latency, high-bandwidth, and latency-sensitive applications. This ensures that each connected device or application receives the appropriate level of service without impacting others.
    • Improved Overall System Performance: By ensuring efficient resource utilization and QoS, dynamic port arbitration contributes to improved overall system performance, leading to better end-user experiences, reduced latencies, and increased throughput for data-intensive applications.

    In summary, dynamic port arbitration in the PCIe switches is vital for PowerMax’s ability to ensure efficient resource utilization, providing QoS for critical applications, enabling flexibility and scalability, supporting diverse workloads, and ultimately improving the overall system performance.

    Hardware Security

    The cybersecurity threat profile continually evolves and expands to new areas. In recent years the component supply chain and the firmware these components use has become an attractive attack vector. There are documented cases of malicious hardware and compromised firmware being deliberately inserted into systems at the component factory compromising their security even before they reach the customer floor. PowerMax has a number of protection mechanisms to providing customers, the highest level of security to guard against compromised supply chain components and firmware.

    PowerMax compute node architecture has implemented the following security strategies:

    Hardware Root of Trust

    PowerMax 2500/8500 arrays use an immutable, silicon-based Hardware Root-of-Trust (HWRoT) to cryptographically affirm the integrity of BIOS and BMC firmware. This root-of-trust is based on one-time programmable, read-only public keys provisioned by Dell in the factory to provide protection against malware tampering.

    The BIOS boot process uses Intel Boot Guard technology which verifies that the digital signature of the cryptographic hash of the boot image matches the signature stored in silicon by Dell in the factory. If Boot Guard validates successfully, the rest of the BIOS firmware modules are validated by using a chain of trust procedure until control is handed off to PowerMax OS 10.

    Each BIOS module contains a hash of the next module in the chain. The key modules in BIOS are the IBB (Initial Boot Block), SEC (Security), PEI (Pre-EFI Initialization), MRC (Memory Reference Code), DXE (Driver Execution Environment), and BDS (Boot Device Selection). If Intel Boot Guard authenticates the IBB (Initial Boot Block), then the IBB validates SEC+PEI before handing control to it. SEC+PEI then validates PEI+MRC which further validates the DXE+BDS modules resulting in control being handed over to UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) Secure Boot. Rapid recovery to a trusted image is implemented on the PowerMax platform when authentication fails. The rapid recovery is essential within the HWRoT implementation and is automatically initiated by the BMC to guarantee maximum security and uptime is maintained.

    Secure Boot

    Secure Boot represents an industry-wide standard for security in the pre-boot environment. Computer system vendors, expansion card vendors, and operating system providers collaborate on the specification to promote interoperability. Secure boot is the process of verification that the image to be booted is exactly the image that is expected. It is used during Hardware Root of Trust, firmware load, and firmware upgrade as well as extended through all the various images needed to be booted all the way through the execution of the OS image such as bootloaders to firmware to Initial BIOS to UEFI.

    PowerMaxOS 10 for PowerMax 2500/8500 supports industry standard UEFI Secure Boot which checks the cryptographic signatures of UEFI drivers, kernels and other code loaded prior to the OS running. UEFI Secure Boot prevents unsigned (untrusted) UEFI device drivers or OS kernels from being loaded, displays error messages, and does not allow the device to function.

    Measured Boot

    Measured Boot is the process of storing hash values used for authentication during a secure boot sequence. Values are stored in the boot log within a TCG-defined trusted platform module (TPM), public keys, and the various signatures. The TPM values can be used via a token process by an upstream OS or applications to validate the expected execution of a secure boot process. PowerMaxOS 10 for PowerMax 2500/8500 supports two versions of TPM:

    • TPM 2.0 FIPS + Common Criteria + TCG certified
    • TPM 2.0 China certified

    The TPM can be used to perform public key cryptographic functions, compute hash functions, generate, manage, and securely store keys.

    Secure Firmware Upgrade

    PowerMax uses digital signatures on firmware updates for all components and sub-components to assure that only authentic firmware is running on the platform. Secure firmware upgrade uses cryptographic authentication of digital signatures applied to the firmware bootloader and images of the running firmware prior to running any update process.

    Enhanced firmware authentication is embedded within many third-party devices which provide signature validation using their own Root-of-Trust mechanisms. This prevents the possible use of a compromised third-party update tool from being used to load malicious firmware into, for example, a NIC or storage drive (and bypassing the use of signed Dell update packages). Many of the third-party PCIe and storage devices shipped with PowerMax use a hardware Root-of-Trust to validate their respective firmware updates.

    If any firmware in any device is suspected of malicious tampering, Administrators can roll back the platform firmware images to an earlier trusted version stored in PowerMax.

The next generation PowerMax systems run a completely redesigned version of operating system software called PowerMaxOS 10. The latest PowerMaxOS 10 software builds on decades of software innovation that has provided the most trusted, intelligent, secure storage platform in the industry for demanding mission-critical workloads. PowerMaxOS 10 builds on the mission critical foundation of its predecessors bringing forth new enhancements, it is more efficient at managing cache memory resources reducting the amount of required DRAM cache for these systems reducing the total cost of ownership (TCO) long term. PowerMax OS 10 incorporates AI and machine learning capabilities that offer intelligent insights through smart analytics and predictive insights, enabling proactive performance tuning and capacity planning.

PowerMaxOS Advanced Quality of Service Features (QoS)

  • In modern datacenter environments, applications and workloads may have different performance requirements, often using a SAN environment which could be comprised of multiple generations of equipment (HBAs, switches, and storage arrays). These mixed environments produce challenges when trying to deliver the consistent performance levels enterprise applications require. To help deliver a consistent performance level for applications deployed in these diverse environments, PowerMaxOS employs powerful QoS features in the following ways:

    • Service levels provide open systems customers with the ability to separate applications based on performance requirements and business importance. PowerMaxOS provides the ability to set specified service levels to ensure the highest priority application response times are not impacted by lower priority applications. Service levels address the requirements of customers to ensure that applications have a predictable, and consistent, level of performance while running on the array. The available service levels are defined in PowerMaxOS and can be applied to an application’s storage group at any time. This allows for the Storage Administrator to initially set, as well as change, the performance level of an application as needed.
    • Host I/O Limits is a feature that can be used to limit the amount of front-end (FE) bandwidth and I/Os per second (IOPs) that can be consumed by a set of devices over a set of OR  ports. Setting host I/O limits allows a user to define front end port performance limits on a storage group. These front-end limits can be set by IOPS, host MB per host, or a combination of both. Host I/O limits can be set on storage group that has a specified service level to throttle IOPS on applications that are exceeding expected service level desired performance. 
    • Initiator Bandwidth Limits is a feature which can be used to mitigate a well-known class of performance problem inherent to all lossless storage transport protocols called “Slow Drain”. Slow drains on a fabric can occur for a variety of reasons but often they stem from a mismatch between the maximum link speeds supported by an initiator and target. This mismatch in link speeds is often seen in SAN fabrics which use multiple generations of equipment, such as when a new 32 Gb FC storage array is provisioned to legacy hosts which use slower speed 8 Gb FC HBAs. In this case, the data coming out of the new 32 Gb FC storage port could quickly overrun the processing ability of the 8 Gb HBA. Because of inherent Fibre Channel flow controls, the 32 Gb FC storage port would halt transferring frames until the 8 Gb HBA had cleared enough so it could start receiving frames again. Other hosts which are provisioned storage from the 32 Gb FC port would see a degradation in throughput and overall performance during this time. PowerMaxOS Initiator Bandwidth Limits, along with PowerMaxOS support for Fabric Performance Impact Notifications (FPINs), address this problem. Initiator Bandwidth Limits throttles the amount of throughput a PowerMax storage port can deliver to a host initiator so that the storage port will not over run the initiator’s capabilities to process the incoming data. Initiator bandwidth limits are placed on an initiator group and only affect the initiators within the group. Other initiators which are using the storage port are unaffected and will still receive data at unthrottled speeds.

    All PowerMax QoS features can be applied using traditional PowerMax management tools (Unisphere for PowerMax, REST API, and Solutions Enabler). PowerMaxOS QoS features are available at no additional cost for all PowerMax models.

    PowerMax AIOps

    Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations (AIOps), or Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations, plays a crucial role in modern storage operations by leveraging AI and machine learning to enhance efficiency, performance, and reliability. As data grows exponentially and become more diverse, traditional manual processes for managing storage resources become increasingly inadequate.

PowerProtect Data Manager (PPDM)

  • The role of PowerProtect Data Manager (PPDM) in this integration is pivotal, orchestrating storage group and device-level snapshot backups from PowerMax 2500/8500 arrays directly to PowerProtect appliances. Key features of PPDM include centralized management and a simple, intuitive user interface that allows for the orchestration of backups and recoveries efficiently. The backups can be configured for either crash-consistent or application-consistent states, catering to various application needs. The flexibility of restores is also enhanced, allowing recoveries to be made to the primary production Storage Group, another Storage Group on the same PowerMax array, or to a Storage Group on a secondary PowerMax array.

    To review, PPDM brings the following core features to the solution:

    • Centralized Management: PPDM provides a simple, intuitive user interface for the centralized management and orchestration of backups and recoveries, enhancing existing storage environments.
    • Fast Incremental Backups: Backups using PPDM can be configured for either crash-consistent or application-consistent states, catering to the needs of different applications and databases.
    • Flexible Restore Options: Fast recovery options allow restores to the primary production Storage Group, another Storage Group on the same PowerMax array, or to a Storage Group on a secondary PowerMax array.

    PPDM Management Dashboard

    Advanced features provided by PPDM further enhance its utility. Users benefit from file support for both block and file workloads, ensuring compatibility across diverse data environments. Backups can be encrypted and stored immutably, significantly enhancing data security. Additionally, the capability to replicate backups between physical or virtual DD/DDVE appliances ensures effective data redundancy strategies. Cloud tiering, as part of a broader multicloud strategy, optimizes data management and storage efficiency.

    To review, leveraging PPDM includes access to several advanced features:

    • File Support: PPDM supports both block and file workloads, accommodating diverse data environments.
    • Encrypted and Immutable Backups: Backups are encrypted and stored immutably, ensuring enhanced security and protection against data loss.
    • Replication Capabilities: Users can replicate backups between physical or virtual DD/DDVE appliances, ensuring effective data redundancy strategies.
    • Cloud Tiering: As part of a broader multicloud strategy, cloud tiering capabilities further optimize data management and storage efficiency.

    In summary, the Storage Direct Protection feature for PowerMax is a transformative solution for data protection, delivering efficiency, flexibility, and high performance. By enabling seamless backups to PowerProtect DD appliances with no performance impact on applications, organizations can experience rapid backup and restore operations, exceptional data reduction ratios, and the ability to strategically manage backups across multiple cloud platforms. Coupled with the powerful capabilities of PowerProtect Data Manager, this integration empowers businesses to develop comprehensive multicloud data protection strategies that enhance operational efficacy and business continuity.

Recovery

Several options also exist for native cyber recovery from a secure vault for open systems and mainframe storage on PowerMax.

Remote replication with SRDF

  • Symmetrix Remote Data Facility (SRDF) is one of the most popular data services in the enterprise data center and is considered the gold standard for remote replication. Up to 70% of Fortune 500 companies use SRDF to replicate their critical data to geographically dispersed data centers throughout the world. SRDF offers customers the ability to replicate tens of thousands of volumes, with each volume being replicated to a maximum of four different locations globally.

    PowerMaxOS 10 runs an enhanced version of SRDF specific for all flash use cases. This version uses multi-core, multi-threading techniques to boost performance; and powerful write folding algorithms to greatly reduce replication bandwidth requirements along with source and target array back-end writes to flash.

    There are four types of SRDF:

    • SRDF Synchronous (SRDF/S) – SRDF/S delivers zero data loss remote mirroring between data centers separated by up to 120 miles (200 km).
    • SRDF Asynchronous (SRDF/A) – SRDF/A delivers asynchronous remote data replication between data centers up to 8000 miles (12875 km) apart. SRDF/S and SRDF/A can be used together to support three or four site topologies as required by the world’s most mission-critical applications.
    • SRDF/Metro – SRDF/Metro delivers active-active high availability for non-stop data access and workload mobility within a data center, or between data centers separated by up to 60 miles (100 km). SRDF/Metro allows for storage array clustering, enabling even more resiliency, agility, and data mobility. SRDF/Metro allows hosts or host clusters access to LUNs replicated between two different sites. The hosts can see both views of the Metro Replicated LUN (R1 and R2), but it appears to the host OS as if it were the same LUN. The host can then write to both the R1 and R2 devices simultaneously. This use case accounts for automated recovery and the seamless failover of applications thus avoiding recovery scenarios altogether. Other key features of SRDF Metro are:
    • It provides concurrent access of LUNS /storage groups for non-stop data access and higher availability across metro distances.
    • It delivers simpler and seamless data mobility.
    • It supports stretch clustering which is ideal for Microsoft and VMware environments.
    • SRDF/Metro Smart DR – SRDF/Metro can provide additional levels of data resiliency and efficiency by incorporating intelligent software (Smart DR) that allows both primary PowerMax sites (R1 and R2) to send a single copy of data to a shared DR site via asynchronous replication, resulting in the following benefits:
    • Increased resiliency: if one of the primary PowerMax arrays becomes unavailable, DR operations continue with the surviving primary PowerMax array.
    • Increased efficiency: a single DR copy for both SRDF/Metro arrays and data that is only sent from one side to the DR array. This results in space and bandwidth efficiency.

Scalability

  • Scalability is a crucial aspect of AIOPs (Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations) because it enables the platform to handle increasing workloads and volumes of data without a corresponding increase in infrastructure or resources. As the volume of data and the number of devices under management grow, a single PowerMax array can have up to 64K user accessible devices. AIOPs must be able to scale horizontally to ensure that it can continue to process and analyze the data in real-time, providing accurate insights and enabling efficient decision-making. Without scalability, AIOPs would quickly become overwhelmed, leading to decreased performance, increased latency, and reduced accuracy.

    Scalability allows AIOPs to adapt to changing business needs, handle unexpected spikes in traffic, and provide continuous monitoring and analytics capabilities. Moreover, scalability enables organizations to leverage the full potential of AIOPs, enabling them to achieve greater efficiency, reduce costs, and improve overall business outcomes. By providing real-time visibility and automation, scalable AIOPs can help organizations respond quickly to changing conditions, mitigate risks, and optimize IT operations, ultimately driving business success.

    PowerMax REST API is ever evolving, with each release new efficiencies are introduced  PowerMax REST API is a function of the Unisphere for PowerMax management software suite, upgrades provide users with the latest functionality while preserving interoperability with previous 2 releases of the API. This forward compatibility gives developers time to validate against newer versions of the API and adopt new features without fear upgrades will break their existing automation. 

    REST API for PowerMax version 10.1 introduced the greatest scalability feature to date, a new enhanced API that enables developers to gather large amounts of data for multiple storage objects with few or a single API call. 

    Enhanced API calls have been introduced for:

    • Performance Data Reporting
    • Storage Group Configuration and associated configuration, including replication details for Snapshots and SRDF configurations
    • Volume Configuration – Including all volume related attributes

    Advanced attribute selection and filtering make the New Enhanced API calls even more flexible enabling complex use cases with a single API call. What’s more is that New Enhanced Performance API calls greatly simplify the process of retrieving performance data since the calls are GET and don’t require any payload to be calculated by the developer for the API to retrieve data. For more information, please refer to InfoHub blogs here.

Secure Snapshots

  • Secure snaps are an optional setting for SnapVX targetless snapshots that prevent a user from deleting snapshots accidentally or intentionally and are retained in resource-limited situations in which conventional snaps are placed into a failed state to release resources. The best protection is provided by a combination of conventional snaps for frequent points-in-time for granular recovery options, and less frequent secure snaps for increased protection and resiliency to recover for more critical situations caused by severe application issues and malicious attacks. For more information please refer to the SnapVX Technical Note.

The Dynamic Fabric

  • Both the PowerMax 2500 and 8500 are architected using an internal NVMe-oF topologies. These NVMe-oF topologies in the next generation platform are referred to as the PowerMax “Dynamic Fabric”. The dynamic fabric turns the compute and backend storage elements into individual independent endpoints on a large internal storage area network (SAN). The dynamic fabric allows these individual compute and storage endpoints to be placed into shared logical and physical resource pools, which in turn disaggregates the storage and compute resources in the system. In this architecture, all node endpoints can access all storage endpoints in the DMEs using the system’s high speed NVMe-oF topologies, creating a true “active/active and share everything” system architecture. This system disaggregation decouples the compute and storage so that they be scaled and provisioned independently of each other to meet application requirements rather than adhering to strict system architecture requirements. This disaggregated architecture makes the new PowerMax systems:

    • Much more efficient storage system regarding resource utilization when delivering the required workload performance and storage capacity for applications, all the while consuming less power.
    • Much easier to scale up and scale out.
    • Able to achieve the same high levels of fault tolerance and resiliency without the need for costly additional hardware.

    Being a true active/active architecture allows nodes to freely access the data in another node’s memory. On PowerMax this is done by using Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA). Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) is the ability of reading from and writing to memory on a remote machine without interrupting the processing of the CPU(s) on that system. RDMA permits high-throughput, low-latency data transfer between the memory of two computing systems which is essential in massively parallel high performing computing systems like PowerMax. Using RDMA, all PowerMax nodes can access the memory contents of any other remote node in the system as if it were local to the node. The ability for each node to access other nodes memory using RDMA turns the total capacity of cache in the PowerMax systems into a shared pool resource called PowerMax Global Cache.

    Note: For each node, the memory of the other nodes is accessible as if it was its own, but the communication does incur some fabric latency (around 0.7us) making the PowerMax a Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) system.

    A key requirement for PowerMax Global Cache is that the fabric which transports the internode RDMA communications must be extremely low latency and have very high bandwidth. For this reason, PowerMax uses the InfiniBand protocol as its primary internode fabric. InfiniBand fabrics, such as NVIDIA’s Quantum, provide native support for RDMA and is a primary reason why they are specifically used in High Performing Computing (HPC) and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions.

    InfiniBand is an industry standard communication transport protocol defined by the InfiniBand Trade Association (IBTA). InfiniBand offers a reliable, lossless, in-order, efficient, connection-oriented transport service implemented at the hardware level. At its core, the InfiniBand specification defines a layer 2 network architecture for communications between servers, switches, and storage subsystems. While certainly not as widespread in the industry as Ethernet based fabrics, its use in HPC environments as a high-performance boutique protocol is a result of four key value propositions:

    • Designed to provide low latency and high bandwidth data transfer with minimum overhead: InfiniBand is designed so that a single lane can transmit up to 100 Gbps (approximately 12.5 GBps) with 4x lanes transmitting up to 400 Gbps (approximately 50 GBps). Current widespread deployed Ethernet 100 Gb solutions require multiple lanes (i.e. 4 x 25 Gb). Larger single lane data transfer is more efficient than smaller multilane data transfer as more data is transferred using a single clock cycle – consuming less resources to transfer the same amount of data.

    Note: In February 2021, IEEE 802.3cu standard was approved which defined single lane 100 GbE. The widespread implementation of this standard onto industry hardware is expected to occur post 2025.

    • High energy efficiency: The PowerMax InfiniBand fabric is run in “Connection Mode” which supports MTU sizes of up to 2 GB. In connection mode, studies have shown that InfiniBand is over 70% more energy efficient per byte sent than other RDMA fabric choices such as Ethernet 1 https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7027477
    • Scalability: InfiniBand is highly scalable as it can support tens of thousands of fabric endpoints in a single subnet network. A core tenent of the next generation PowerMax architecture is to move from being “bus centric” to “endpoint centric”. Being endpoint centric is the foundation for system disaggregation where thousands of endpoints (be either compute or storage) can communicate with all other endpoints over a high speed “flat” network. A flat network is critical for disaggregated architectures as needing to route traffic over multiple subnets adds unwanted latency. InfiniBand’s ability to support tens of thousands of endpoints using a single subnet allows for PowerMax to scale by adding independent compute and storage endpoints into the fabric without having to add additional subnets incurring additional latency penalties.  
    • High Security: InfiniBand has many built in security features. InfiniBand protocols are implemented in hardware and the communication attributes are configured centrally in a way that does not enable software applications to gain control over them and maliciously change those attributes. In addition, each node and port are identified through a 64-bit Global unique identifier (GUID) maintained by hardware, helping to avoid impersonation. In Ethernet, a MAC can be changed via software to impersonate another machine, or a packet can be pre-constructed in software. In InfiniBand, crafting malicious packets in software or changing hardware addressing is basically impossible – such packets will be discarded either by the switch or HCA’s. Here is how InfiniBand handles some of the more common Ethernet based attacks:
      • MAC Flooding - MAC flooding attacks are targeted denial-of-service attacks designed to get the switch to fail open. In InfiniBand MAC Flooding is not possible since the forwarding tables are defined explicitly.
      • ARP Attacks – ARP attacks ARP attacks involve using a known MAC and IP address of a host on a remote VLAN to get the switch to forward packets. In InfiniBand, MACs cannot be compromised as they are derived from the InfiniBand GUID and burned into silicon of the Host Channel Adapter (HCA) card. Also, since InfiniBand is an in-order packet delivery protocol, an attacker would need to acquire the proper queue number and sequence number to insert a malicious packet into the data stream. This would be impossible as by the time the attacker was able to get this information, the next packet with the correct sequence number would have been generated and sent. The InfiniBand fabric would flag the malicious packet as being out of order and it would be dropped by any HCA card as it was received.
      • Tagging Attacks - Attempt to get the switch to forward frames from one VLAN to another. In InfiniBand tagging is handled by the hardware, a node cannot determine its partition (P_Key) only the index. Also, the partitioning is defined on all the switch ports which eliminates the possibility of that port sending a tag which is not allowed to send.
      • VLAN hopping using Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) – VLAN hopping is not possible as InfiniBand does not use spanning tree protocol.

    Using RDMA and NVMe-oF with an IB fabric architecture, the PowerMax Dynamic Fabric delivers the high levels of performance, scalability, efficiency, and security to its enterprise customers require. How the Dynamic Fabric has been implemented to achieve this differs between the PowerMax 2500 and PowerMax 8500.

    PowerMax 2500 Dynamic Fabric

    The PowerMax 2500 is designed to deliver a balance of high performance and power efficiency in a compact package. A PowerMax 2500 system can scale up to two node pairs providing up to 128 CPU cores (64 in each node pair) and up to 15.36 TB (7.68 TB per node pair) of total cache per system. Each node pair comes with its own direct attached PCIe (Peripheral Component Interface Express) DME.

    Each PowerMax 2500 node includes two primary dynamic fabric components:

    • The PowerMax 2500 Back End Module (BEM): The BEM is an IO module whose primary purpose is to manage and facilitate the NVMe data transfer between the node pair and the DME. Each node has a single BEM using a x16 lane PCIe fabric (NVMe/PCIe). This yields a total of 16 GB/s of bidirectional throughput between each node and DME (32 GB/s of total bandwidth between the node pair and DME).

    Note: BEMs are not used on the PowerMax 8500.

    • The PowerMax 2500 Fabric Attach Module (FAM): The FAM is a dual port 100 Gb Host Channel Adapter card (HCA) whose primary purpose is to manage and facilitate the RDMA communication between nodes pairs using an Infiniband fabric (NVMe/IB). Each FAM uses a total of 16 PCIe lanes which are accessbile by both nodes (8 lanes from Node 1 and 8 lanes from Node 2) yielding a total potential of 16 GB/sec of bidirectional throughput for the RDMA traffic between node pairs.

    Note: FAMs are added into the system only when a second node pair is added into the PowerMax 2500 configuration. All RDMA communication between the nodes in a node pair occur on an internal 32 lane PCIe fabric.

    The PowerMax 2500 NVMe/IB fabric is switchless. A key architectural part of the PowerMax 2500 dynamic fabric which enables it to be switchless is the use of PCIe Multihost technology. PCIe Multihost technology is a feature that allows multiple host systems to connect to and share a single PCIe device. This is a useful capability in several fields as sharing high-performance devices like NVMe storage or GPUs among several servers can optimize resource utilization and reduce costs.

    Key points about PCIe Multihost technology include:

    • Resource sharing: Various systems can share resources like GPUs, SSDs, or network adapters to improve cost efficiency and resource utilization.
    • Isolation and security: Even though devices are shared, PCIe multihost ensures that the data traffic and access is isolated, maintaining security between different hosts.
    • Virtualization: By presenting multiple virtual devices from a single physical device, PCIe multihost technology supports robust virtualization platforms and configurations.

    PCIe multihost capability is particularly valuable in high-performance computing (HPC) clusters, data centers, and environments employing virtualization technology where efficient resource allocation is critical. Along with the next generation PowerMax, major players in the industry like Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA use PCIe multihost capabilities for various HPC and Generative AI solutions.

    In the case of the PowerMax 2500, PCIe Multihost allows node pairs to share each other's FAMs, creating a high-speed switchless fabric between the node pairs for low latency RDMA communication. This enables the PowerMax 2500 to scale up and scale out while still maintaining a lower cost switchless fabric profile. The Dynamic Fabric configuration on the PowerMax 2500 allows it to deliver performance and scalability in a compact package. It allows for higher levels of efficiency as the PowerMax 2500 can store up to 7x more capacity (over 4 PBe in 5U) in half the rack space than the previous generation PowerMax 2000.

    PowerMax 2500 Dynamic Fabric

    PowerMax 2500 Scale Up and Scale Out

    As stated earlier, all starter PowerMax 2500 system configuration come with a single node pair and single DME. These systems are referred to as “1x1” systems. The PowerMax 2500 dynamic fabric allows a 1x1 system to scale out by adding an additional node pair without the need for an additional DME. These two-node pair and single DME systems are referred to as “2x1” systems. If the system needs to scale up by adding additional storage, then a second node pair and additional DME are needed. These systems are referred to as “2x2” systems. A single node pair and two DME system (1x2) is not a supported PowerMax 2500 configuration.

    PowerMax 8500 – a fully disagregated storage architecture

    The PowerMax 8500 is designed to provide customers with massive scalability. It can scale up compute from 1 to 8 node pairs (up to 576 CPU cores) while scaling out storage by using 1 to 8 storage Dynamic Media Enclosures (DMEs) to provide over 18 PBe in a single system. On the PowerMax 8500, the dynamic fabric is full end to end NVMe over InfiniBand (NVMe/IB). All internode RDMA communications and data transfers back and forth between the node memory and storage occur over the NVMe/IB fabric. The PowerMax 8500 has implemented the dynamic fabric so that the compute and storage elements of the system are fully disagregated. Each node and storage element are treated as unique endpoints on the InfiniBand fabric. This allows for nodes and storage to added into the fabric independently of each other while being able to access all other endpoints of the fabric be it storage or compute.

    PowerMax 8500 Dynamic Fabric

    Aside from the node pairs and the DMEs,  core components of the PowerMax 8500 dynamic fabric are:

    • PowerMax 8500 Fabric Attach Module (FAM) – All PowerMax 8500 nodes connect into the dynamic fabric using a single Host Channel Adapter (HCA). These node HCAs are the PowerMax 8500 Fabric Attach Modules (FAM). On the PowerMax 8500, each FAM contains dual 100 Gb QSFP28 InfiniBand ports. Each PowerMax 8500 FAM is connected via the chassis midplane to each node’s CPU using a single x16 PCIe connection. This allows for a total of 32 lanes of PCIe connectivity for 32 GBps of bidirectional throughput to the fabric switches from each node. The PowerMax 8500 FAM also features NVMe/IB hardware acceleration as it provides the RDMA data movement between the nodes and drives in the DMEs on the system. The FAM is a hot swappable component and will consume typically around 38 Watts of power.

    PowerMax 8500 Fabric Attach Modules

    The above diagram is a rear view of the PowerMax 8500 3U node pair chassis. Each nodes FAM card is shown. As said earlier, each PowerMax 8500 node will use a single FAM (two total for each node pair). The dual 100 Gbps QSFP ports are visible. Each 100 Gbps ports on the FAM will connect to one of the InfiniBand fabric switches in the system (connecting to either Fabric A or Fabric B).

    • Dual InfiniBand fabrics – The heart of the PowerMax InfiniBand fabric is comprised of two 36 port InfiniBand switches (one for Fabric A and one for Fabric B). Each port on the switch is 100 Gbps QSFP28, allowing for a total aggregate througput of 7.2 Tbps per switch. Each switch features fully redundant host swappable power supplies and cooling fans. The switches are 1U and are shipped mounted and precabled in the PowerMax 8500 rack using Active Optical Cables (AOC) with integrated QSFPs. The switches consume approximately 162 Watts of power each.

    PowerMax 8500 36 port InfiniBand Switch

    Note: Because of the fully disaggregated nature of the PowerMax 8500, the InfiniBand switch pair is required even for a single node pair system. This is a requirement as even though the system has a only single node pair, multiple Dynamic Media Enclosures (DME) can be added independently as the storage needs of the customer scale. The single node pair will be able to communicate with any and all DMEs in the system through the fabrics using the InfiniBand swtiches.

    The InfiniBand switches receive back up power from two Li-Ion system power supplies (SPS). These power supplies are located in the bottom of the first rack of the PowerMax 8500 system. These SPS provide upwards of 5 minutes of run time for the switches to gracefully shutdown in the event of a power failure.

    PowerMax 8500 Li-Ion Backup Power Supply for InfiniBand Switches

    • PowerMax 8500 Dynamic Media Enclosures (DME) – The PowerMax storage DMEs connect into the PowerMax 8500 InfiniBand fabric using two Link Control Cards (LCC) - one for Fabric A another for Fabric B. Each LCC contains a dual port 100 Gbps InfiniBand HCA. Each 100 Gbps port connects into the InfiniBand switch on either Fabric A or Fabric B.

    In terms of NVMe/IB fabrics, the LCC acts as the storage endpoint on the fabric where a compute node initiator will connect to logical storage controllers. An LCC supports, controls, and monitors the DME, and acts as the primary interconnect between the physical storage and the compute nodes. Each LCC board has its own NVIDIA Bluefield Data Processing Unit (DPU) which feature 16 Arm V8 cores allowing it to perform critical storage management functions such as  fabric offload. The LCCs with their DPUs essentially make each PowerMax 8500 DME a unique active/active dual controller NVMe storage subsystem on the fabric.

    PowerMax 8500 DME LCC

    Note: All PowerMax 8500 systems use Active Optical Cables (AOC) for dynamic fabric connectivity. The intial Dynamic Fabric configuration (number of Node Pairs and number of DMEs) is determined by the customer order. The dynamic fabric configuration arrives at the customer site installed, cabled, and preconfigured from the factory. Nodes and DMEs added into the configuration post installation are done by Dell Technologies field personel.

    PowerMax 8500 Scale Up and Scale Out Configurations

    The Dynamic InfiniBand Fabric allows for the PowerMax 8500 to scale up and scale out with ease. Both compute and storage can be added into the configuration independently of one another based on customer needs.

    All PowerMax 8500 starter configurations contain a single compute node pair, a single storage DME, and two InfiniBand Switches. This is referred to as the starter configuration as shown in the following diagram:

    Basic PowerMax 8500 Starter Configuration

    As a customers needs expand, they can either add compute node pairs and/or storage DME as required. Customers can scale up by adding compute or scale out by adding storage independetnly of each other.

    PowerMax 8500 Scale Up and Scale Out

    The PowerMax 8500 can scale up to six PowerMax node pairs and scale out to four storage DMEs in a single rack as shown in the following diagram.

    PowerMax 8500 maximum single rack configuration

    It is expected that the capabilites of a single PowerMax 8500 rack will supply enough storage compute and capacity for most customer needs; however the system has the capability add a second rack for additional compute and capacity. This second rack can be postitioned up to 25 meters from the first rack. Before adding the second rack, there is a customer decision point where the second rack can either be added in a balanced configuration where it has equal node pairs and DMEs as the first rack. This descision point occurs to when either a fifth node pair or DME is to be added into the configuration. The balanced configuration comprises of four node pairs and four DMEs in each rack, while the unbalanced configuration allows the customer to continue adding to a sixth node pair in the first rack then adding the additional node pairs and DMEs in the second rack. This is shown in the following diagram:

    PowerMax 8500 two rack configurations

    Aside from the additional compute nodes and DMEs, the second rack does not require any additional IB switches, or additional system power supplies.

    Note: The terminology balanced vs unbalanced only refers to the quantiy of node pairs and DMEs in both PowerMax 8500 racks. The PowerMax 8500 is designed so that the workload can be spread evenly across all PowerMax 8500 components regardless if the two rack system is either a balanced or unbalanced configuration.

    As said earlier, the PowerMax 8500 can be configured to meet a variety of customer needs. Its disagregated nature makes it so that compute and storage can be added independently of each other. The Dynamic Media Enclosure

  • The next generation PowerMax uses a newly designed disk storage enclosure called the Dynamic Media Enclosure (DME). The next generation PowerMax DME is designed to maximize storage density, supporting up to 48, side loading, high capacity 2.5” NVMe SSDs allowing for up to over 4 PBe in a 2U form factor. Side loading drive carriers, also known as horizontal drive carriers, offer advantages in terms of storage capacity per rack unit compared to other drive carrier orientations. Side loading drive carriers allow for a higher density of drives within a given rack unit. By positioning the drives horizontally, side by side, the rack unit is fully utilized in terms of width, height, and depth. Drives can be layered across the entire depth and width of the enclosure rather than being only limited to its width. By layering drives in this manner, more capacity per rack unit can be achieved as more drives can be added without having to increase the height of the enclosure.

    Next Generation 2U PowerMax DME (rear view)

    The next generation PowerMax supports a variety of NVMe SSD capacity sizes (3.84 TB, 7.68 TB, 15.36 TB, and 30.72 TB). Drive sizes can be intermixed within a DME with the only requirement that the drives be one size apart (i.e., 3.84 TB drives can be intermixed with 7.68 TB drives).

    PowerMax DME Enhanced Adaptive Cooling

    The side loading nature of the DME allows for an innovative thermal design which effectively manages the increased heat generated it’s high-density NVMe SSD configuration. The new DME uses an adaptive cooling design featuring six variable speed fan packs, each with dual 60 mm fans, which push a high velocity airflow from the front of the unit, around the sides of the NVMe SSD drives, and out the back of the enclosure. The fan packs variable speeds are controlled by an onboard BMC and sensors which are constantly measuring air pressure, air speed, and temperatures within the unit and of each individual NVMe SSD in the enclosure.

    Next Generation PowerMax DME (top view)

    The next generation PowerMax DME has its fan packs mounted in the front of the enclosure creating a high velocity airflow which traverses the enclosure from the front to the back. With high density storage systems such as the next generation PowerMax, airflow is of paramount importance in the drive enclosures as proper airflow plays a crucial role in maintaining optimal operating temperatures, ensuring the reliability and longevity of the drives, and maximizing overall system performance. This airflow along with the side loading alignment of the drives greatly improves the heat dissipation of the unit as the drive carriers are aligned with the airflow and not perpendicular to it. This provides several additional cooling efficiency advantages over traditional enclosures with the drives in the front and fans in the rear. Some of these advantages are:

    • Airflow Direction: Front-facing fans pull in cool air from the front of the enclosure, where ambient air temperatures are typically lower. This allows the fans to draw in fresh, cooler air directly onto the drives and other components, facilitating more efficient cooling. Rear fans, on the other hand, often face warmer air due to the heat generated by the components within the enclosure.
    • Heat Dissipation: Drives in an enclosure tend to generate heat predominantly on their front-facing side where the circuitry and components are located. Front-facing fans are positioned to target this area directly, allowing for efficient heat dissipation. Rear fans, while still contributing to overall airflow, may not provide as focused cooling to the front side of the drives, potentially resulting in less effective heat dissipation.
    • Hot Spot Prevention: Front-facing fans help prevent the formation of hot spots within the enclosure  byevenly distributing airflow across all drives, minimizing temperature variations and preventing localized heat concentrations. This is particularly important in high-density storage environments such as the next generation PowerMax where the drives are closely packed together.
    • Maintenance Accessibility: Front-facing fans can be easily accessed and cleaned without the need to remove drives or other components. This accessibility ensures that the fans can be kept free from dust and debris, optimizing their cooling performance.

    In summary, airflow management is critical for high-capacity drive enclosures such as the PowerMax DME to maintain optimal operating temperatures, extend drive lifespan, and ensure reliable performance. The DME’s advanced airflow and innovative active cooling design contributes to the overall system stability, reduces the risk of failures, and helps customers maximize the value and longevity of their storage infrastructure.

The GuestOS

  • PowerMaxOS uses a real-time, non-disruptive storage hypervisor that manages and protects embedded services by extending high availability to services that traditionally would have run external to the array. This storage hypervisor is called the GuestOS.

    The GuestOS is a lightweight hypervisor that virtualizes the PowerMax node hardware (CPU cores, internal network, and memory) for the deployment of various application containers directly on the internal PowerMax infrastructure. The typical applications which run in these containers are embedded Unisphere for PowerMax, VMware’s vStorage APIs for Storage Awareness (VASA) provider, and Software Defined Network Attached Storage (SDNAS). The following is a brief description of these containerized applications:

    • Embedded Unisphere for PowerMax (eMGMT) provides a highly available implementation of the Unisphere for PowerMax Management software suite. This eMGMT has full functionality of Unisphere for managing your PowerMax arrays without deploying additional hardware resources. eMGMT provides a web based UI with all management and performance monitoring capabilites, a full REST API, and the ability to configure CLI over IP with Client/Server configuration to the eMGMT guest.
    • VASA is a set of APIs developed by VMware to provide storage awareness to VMware environments, enabling better integration between virtual machines and storage solutions. VASA allows storage providers to communicate storage-related information, such as performance metrics, capabilities, and status, to the VMware vSphere environment.
    • Dell's SDNAS is a storage architecture that combines the flexibility and scalability of software-defined storage with the accessibility and simplicity of network-attached storage. SDNAS allows organizations to utilize various storage resources, manage them through software, and provide shared access to data over a network.

    The GuestOS dynamically allocates node CPU core resources for the compute needs for the containers. Memory is allocated to the containers in a similar way from each nodes cache. The GuestOS containers can access the system storage using a virtual host bus adapter called a Cut Through Device (CTD). A single CTD will be setup for each node in the system by the GuestOS and up to 32 virtual ports (logical ports 32 – 63) can be set up on the CTD which are specifically used by the containers for high-speed access to system storage. The containers can access multiple virtual Network Interface Card (vNIC) instances established by the GuestOS. These vNICs are associated with various physical ports on MSM and are assigned an internal system IP address. The GuestOS uses Network Address Translation (NAT) to provide translation services between external management network IP addresses assigned by the customer to the internal system IP addresses assigned to the vNICs.

    Primary components of the PowerMax GuestOS

The next generation PowerMax Products

  • Since their 2018 launch, the PowerMax 2000 and 8000 systems have become essential in enterprise data centers, supporting the global digital economy. By 2022, demands for greater power efficiency, performance, security, and automation surged. To stay competitive, organizations needed to speed up data creation to innovation. However, they faced challenges like exponential data growth, diverse and distributed data, internal silos, cybersecurity threats, productivity issues, and cloud complexity.

    To tackle these challenges, organizations required a reliable and innovative storage platform that balances performance, power efficiency, security, and reliability at scale. In response, Dell introduced the next-generation PowerMax 2500 and 8500 systems in 2022, succeeding the original PowerMax 2000 and 8000 models.

    Note: Both the PowerMax 2000 and 8000 are scheduled for end of life on October 31, 2024

    The next generation PowerMax systems are offered in two distinct models, each with its own target use case and price point.

    At a high level:

    • The PowerMax 2500 delivers a balance of high performance and power efficiency in a compact package delivering over 2.5x the IOPS/watt while storing up to 7x more capacity (8 PBe) in half the rack space compared with previous PowerMax 2000. Along with its high efficiency design, the 2500 supports the full complement of rich data services for open systems, mainframe, file, and virtual environments. The PowerMax 2500 excels in rack scale/pod style implementations for mission critical application.
    • The PowerMax 8500 delivers leading performance at scale for the most demanding mixed workloads requiring reliable and predictable performance delivering over 18 PBe of capacity with up to 256 front end ports to customers. When compared to the previous PowerMax 8000, the 8500 delivers up to 2x faster performance and 50% lower response times. Like the PowerMax 2500, the 8500 can easily consolidate open systems, mainframe, file, and virtualized storage to simplify operations, significantly reduce TCO and increase ROI. The PowerMax 8500 excels in the role at being the ideal mission critical workload storage consolidator for an entire enterprise data center.

    The foundation of the next generation PowerMax systems is comprised of five essential elements, which collectively form the cornerstone of the value propositions the platform brings to customers. These key components include:

    • A Future Proof Architecture: An architecture that enables the PowerMax systems to deliver a balance of exceptional performance, efficiency, security, and reliability to customers over the entire lifecycle of the product without requiring significant hardware upgrades.
    • PowerMax OS 10: A sophisticated operating system that powers the system, providing a robust and secure foundation for data management and processing.
    • PowerMax AIOPs: Advanced Intelligent Operations and Performance software driven by artificial intelligence and machine learning that enables real-time monitoring, analytics, and optimization of system performance, ensuring optimal resource allocation and efficiency.
    • PowerMax Cybersecurity: A comprehensive cybersecurity solution that protects the system and its data from potential threats, ensuring the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of critical information.
    • PowerMax Multicloud Mobility: A feature that enables seamless integration with multiple cloud environments, allowing for seamless data management, migration, and orchestration across different cloud platforms.

    These five elements work in unison on the next generation PowerMax platform to provide enterprise customers for a robust and reliable solution to their data storage needs well into the late 2020s. The remainder of this paper will discuss these elements in some detail.

The PowerMax customer

  • Since its introduction in 2018, PowerMax has become a go to platform for the mission critical applications run by enterprise customers. As of the time of writing this paper the PowerMax platform is used by:

    • 95% of the Fortune 500 companies
    • The top 10 US Banks
    • The top 10 Global Health Care companies

    Its proliferation in the data center has made PowerMax a vital component not just to enterprise customer, but to the overall global economy as without PowerMax:

    • Credit card transaction would probably stop working (PowerMax is used for most critical credit card transaction systems)
    • Trains/Automobiles/Planes probably wouldn’t run (PowerMax is used to support the most critical transportation systems such as flight path tracking)
    • The US Government wouldn’t be able to collect taxes or to provide any services to the nation that use tax revenues.
    • Stock Trading would slow if not completely stop (PowerMax is used to support the critical banking systems around the world that clear all sorts of inter-bank and equity-trading systems).

What is the PowerMax Family

  • The PowerMax Family represent the flagship products of Dell’s enterprise storage business. It is designed with a multi-node, active/active scale-out architecture using industry standard, end-to-end NVMe components. The platform features inline, global dedupe and compression, providing customers with high storage efficiency even as the system scales. The PowerMax family also provides what many consider to be the gold standard in data services, proven high availability and resiliency, and advanced security that adheres to stringent government regulations and corporate compliance requirements like FIPS 140-2. A core strength of the PowerMax family is its ability to consolidate workloads. Customers can use a single PowerMax system for Mainframe and Open Systems block storage, as well providing file storage services as well.

Why customers chose PowerMax

  • Customers choose and rely on PowerMax for their most intense and business critical workloads because of its key value propositions which is to provide a trusted, proven, intelligent, efficient, secure, scalable, and simple to use enterprise storage platform.

    IT executives prioritize value propositions that ensure their data centers, both current and next-gen, can run mission-critical applications with maximum availability. They understand that even minor outages or security breaches can result in significant financial losses. Dell, as a customer-focused company, guarantees that choosing PowerMax for storage will be a decision executives can trust without hesitation.
